messages.content: Why is Korean written in little blocks instead of a straight line of letters like English?

Because Korean is not an alphabet that marches in a line — it is an alphabet that assembles into syllables. Every Korean syllable is one block containing two to four letters (jamo): an initial consonant, a vowel, and optionally a final consonant underneath. Take 학교 (hak-gyo, 'school'): 학 is ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄱ stacked into one square, and 교 is ㄱ + ㅛ. The block is exactly one beat of sound, so Korean text visually pulses in syllables the way English speech pulses in beats you never see.

The practical payoff: once you can read the roughly 40 jamo, you can sound out any block, even a word you have never seen. The layout is logical, too — the vowel sits to the right of or below the initial consonant depending on its shape, and the final consonant (batchim) always goes at the bottom. Learn the stacking rules once and the whole writing system opens up.
Can you lay out the ten basic Korean vowels for me? I keep mixing up the ones with extra strokes.

The ten basic vowels form five pairs: a plain vowel and a 'y' version made by adding one short stroke. Here they are with Revised Romanization:

| Vowel | Sound | Vowel | Sound |
|---|---|---|---|
| ㅏ | a | ㅑ | ya |
| ㅓ | eo | ㅕ | yeo |
| ㅗ | o | ㅛ | yo |
| ㅜ | u | ㅠ | yu |
| ㅡ | eu | ㅣ | i |

Two pronunciation warnings. First, ㅓ (eo) is not the English 'uh' exactly — it is a more open, relaxed 'aw'-like sound, and romanizing it as 'eo' makes beginners say 'ee-oh,' which is wrong; it is one smooth syllable. Second, ㅡ (eu) has no English equivalent at all: say 'oo' with your lips spread flat instead of rounded. The extra-stroke rule is beautifully regular — one added stroke adds a 'y' glide — so ㅑ, ㅕ, ㅛ, ㅠ are never new sounds to memorize, just ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ with a running start.
What exactly is batchim? My textbook keeps warning me about it.

Batchim (받침, literally 'support' or 'prop') is the final consonant that sits at the bottom of a syllable block. Korean syllables can end in a consonant, and that closing consonant is written underneath the vowel: 밥 (bap, 'rice/meal') is ㅂ + ㅏ + ㅂ, where the second ㅂ is the batchim.

Here is the part that calms learners down: although many consonants can be written in batchim position, only seven sounds are ever pronounced there — ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅇ. Everything flattens into one of those seven. So 옷 (clothes) is pronounced [옫], and 부엌 (kitchen) is pronounced [부억]. You do not need to produce exotic final sounds; you need to recognize that a written ㅅ, ㅈ, ㅌ, or ㅎ at the bottom of a block all come out as a quiet, unreleased ㄷ.

Batchim also drives grammar: particles choose their shape based on whether a batchim is present, which is why 책 takes 은 and 을 while 사과 takes 는 and 를. Master batchim and half of Korean grammar gets easier.
받침이 뭐예요? 예를 들어서 설명해 주세요.

받침은 한 글자의 마지막에 오는 자음이에요. 받침이라는 말은 '아래에서 받친다'는 뜻인데, 실제로 글자를 보면 모음 아래에 자음이 받치고 있는 모양이에요. 예를 들어 '밥'이라는 글자는 ㅂ과 ㅏ, 그리고 마지막 ㅂ으로 이루어져 있는데, 이 마지막 ㅂ이 받침이에요. '책'에서는 ㄱ이 받침이고, '물'에서는 ㄹ이 받침이에요.

받침에서 가장 중요한 점은 발음이에요. 받침 자리는 여러 자음이 올 수 있지만, 소리는 ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅇ 일곱 가지만 나요. 그래서 '옷'은 [옫]으로, '꽃'은 [꼳]으로 발음해요. ㅅ이나 ㅈ이 받침에 오면 모두 ㄷ 소리가 되는 거예요.

또 받침이 있으면 조사도 달라져요. 받침이 있는 '책' 뒤에는 '은'과 '을'이 오고, 받침이 없는 '사과' 뒤에는 '는'과 '를'이 와요. 받침을 잘 알면 읽기도, 문법도 훨씬 쉬워져요.
Why does 먹어요 sound like 'meogeoyo' instead of 'meokeoyo'? The ㄱ seems to move.

It really does move — this is yeoneum (연음), the linking rule, and it is the single most important pronunciation rule in Korean. When a syllable ends in a batchim and the next syllable begins with ㅇ (which is silent at the start of a syllable), the batchim consonant hops over and becomes the onset of the next syllable. 먹어요 is spelled 먹 + 어요, but the ㄱ links forward, giving [머거요]. Same story in 읽어요 [일거요] ('read') and 한국어 [한구거] ('Korean language').

Why? Korean strongly prefers syllables that start with a consonant, and a batchim left behind would be pronounced as a weak, unreleased sound. Linking keeps the consonant crisp and the rhythm smooth. This is also why Korean spelling can look intimidating while the spoken word sounds simple: the spelling preserves the dictionary form 먹다, and the linking rule does the rest automatically. When you read aloud, train your eye to expect the hop whenever you see batchim followed by a syllable starting with ㅇ.
국물 is pronounced 'gungmul'?? Where did the ㅇ come from — I only see ㄱ.

You are hearing bihwa (비화), nasalization: a batchim ㄱ, ㄷ, or ㅂ standing before ㄴ or ㅁ changes into its nasal partner. ㄱ becomes ㅇ, ㄷ becomes ㄴ, and ㅂ becomes ㅁ. So 국물 (soup broth) is ㄱ + ㅁ, and the ㄱ nasalizes: [궁물]. 학년 (school year/grade) is ㄱ + ㄴ, giving [항년]. 십리 (ten ri, an old distance unit) shows the ㅂ member of the family: [심니], where ㅂ nasalizes to ㅁ and the following ㄹ hardens into ㄴ behind it.

The logic is pure articulation economy. A hard oral stop right before a nasal consonant is awkward to produce, so Korean converts the stop into the nasal made at the same position in the mouth — lips give ㅁ, tongue-tip gives ㄴ, back of the tongue gives ㅇ. Nothing is random; the sound slides to the nearest comfortable neighbor. Once you learn the three swaps (ㄱ→ㅇ, ㄷ→ㄴ, ㅂ→ㅁ), a whole class of 'irregular-looking' pronunciations becomes predictable.
학교 comes out 'hak-ggyo' and 좋다 comes out 'jota'. Are those two different rules or the same thing happening?

Two different rules, both triggered by consonants colliding across a syllable boundary. 학교 [학꾜] shows tensification (경음화): after a batchim ㄱ, ㄷ, or ㅂ, a following plain ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ, or ㅈ hardens into its tense twin — so ㄱ+ㄱ gives [ㄲ], and 식당 (restaurant) comes out [식땅]. The batchim essentially lends its tension to the next consonant.

좋다 [조타] shows aspiration instead: ㅎ meets ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, or ㅈ and the two merge into a single aspirated sound — ㅎ+ㄱ = [ㅋ], ㅎ+ㄷ = [ㅌ]. That is why 좋다 is [조타], 놓다 (to put down) is [노타], and 축하 (congratulations) is [추카].

A memory hook: tensification is a stop doubling down; aspiration is ㅎ dissolving into its neighbor and leaving a puff of air behind. Both rules are why Korean spelling and Korean sound are cousins, not twins — and both are completely regular once you spot the boundary pattern.
Teach me a reliable method for decoding a Korean syllable block I've never seen before.

Use the same four steps every time, in order. First, find the vowel: if it is a 'tall' vowel (ㅏ, ㅑ, ㅓ, ㅕ, ㅣ) it sits to the right of the first consonant; if it is a 'wide' vowel (ㅗ, ㅛ, ㅜ, ㅠ, ㅡ) it sits below. Second, read the initial consonant on the left or top. Third, blend consonant + vowel. Fourth, check the bottom: if there is a batchim, close the syllable with one of the seven final sounds (ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅇ).

Watch it work on 글 ('writing/text'). The vowel ㅡ is wide, so it sits under the initial ㄱ: 그. Then the bottom holds ㄹ, closing the syllable: 글 [geul]. Try 한: tall vowel ㅏ beside ㅎ gives 하, batchim ㄴ closes it: 한. And 읽: ㅣ beside ㅇ (silent as an initial, so the syllable starts with the vowel), batchim ㄺ — a double batchim where you pronounce only the ㄱ before a consonant: [익].

Slow is fine. Decoding is a mechanical skill; speed is just the same four steps done a thousand times.
연음이란 무엇인가요? 왜 한국어를 빨리 말하면 단어가 이어져 들려요?

연음은 받침 있는 글자 뒤에 'ㅇ'으로 시작하는 글자가 올 때, 받침이 다음 글자로 넘어가서 소리 나는 현상이에요. 예를 들어 '먹어요'는 글자로는 '먹'과 '어요'이지만, 받침 ㄱ이 넘어가서 [머거요]라고 발음해요. '읽어요'도 [일거요]가 되고, '한국어'도 [한구거]가 돼요.

이런 현상이 생기는 이유는 한국어가 자음으로 시작하는 음절을 편하게 느끼기 때문이에요. 받침을 그대로 두면 소리가 약하고 끊기지만, 다음 음절로 넘기면 발음이 또렷하고 흐름이 부드러워져요. 그래서 한국어를 들으면 단어와 단어가 이어져서 한 덩어리처럼 들리는 거예요.

외국인 학습자에게 연음은 듣기의 열쇠예요. 사전에서 배운 단어와 실제 소리가 다르게 들린다면, 대부분 연음 때문이에요. '밥을'이 [바블]이 되고 '옷이' [오시]가 되는 것처럼, 조사 앞에서도 연음이 일어나니 같이 익혀 두면 좋아요.
Sometimes ㅇ makes an 'ng' sound and sometimes it's silent. How do I know which one it is?

Position decides everything. At the start of a syllable, ㅇ is a silent placeholder — Korean syllables are written with an initial consonant slot, and ㅇ fills it without making a sound, so 아 is just 'a' and 아이 (child) is 'a-i'. At the bottom of a syllable, as batchim, ㅇ is the 'ng' of 'song': 강 (river) is [강] 'gang', and 방 (room) is 'bang'.

The giveaway is visual: if ㅇ sits at the left or top of the block, ignore it; if it sits at the bottom, pronounce 'ng'. This dual life is actually elegant — one letter doing two jobs depending on its seat. One exception to know: ㅇ batchim is the one final consonant that does not link forward. In 강아지 (puppy), the standard pronunciation is [강아지] — the 'ng' stays home instead of hopping into the next syllable the way a ㄱ or ㅂ would. Keep the rule simple: bottom ㅇ = ng, top ㅇ = nothing, and you will read correctly the vast majority of the time.
What's the real difference between ㄷ and ㄸ, or ㅈ and ㅉ? They look like the same letter doubled.

They are tense consonants, and the difference lives in your throat, not your mouth. Plain consonants like ㄷ and ㅈ are pronounced with relaxed vocal folds and a small puff of air. Tense consonants — ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ, ㅉ — are made with the muscles of the throat tightened, no puff of air, and a slightly higher, sharper pitch on the following vowel. To an English ear, tense sounds often resemble the hard consonant after 's' in words like 'steam' or 'school'.

The contrast changes meaning: 달 (moon) vs 딸 (daughter), 사다 (to buy) vs 싸다 (cheap), 자다 (to sleep) vs 짜다 (salty). Korean actually runs a three-way system — plain, tense, and aspirated (ㅌ, ㅊ, ㅋ, ㅍ) — which is one of the genuinely hard parts of Korean pronunciation for English speakers, whose ears are trained for two.

Practice tip: tense consonants feel 'tight and short'. Say 딸 with a squeezed, clipped ㄸ and a crisp vowel, and contrast it with the softer, breathier 달. Record yourself; your mouth will learn faster than your ears at first.
If Korean has an official romanization, why is Seoul spelled that way? And is it gimchi or kimchi?

Because romanization systems are compromises, and some spellings are older than the current system. The official system, Revised Romanization (2000), writes 김치 as 'gimchi' and 부산 as 'Busan'. But 'kimchi' spread worldwide under the older McCune–Reischauer tradition and sheer usage, and food words tend to keep the spelling the world learned first. 'Seoul' is older still — a conventional European spelling that predates any Korean government system; under Revised Romanization it would be 'Seoul' anyway only by coincidence of convention, since 서울 is pronounced [서울] 'Seo-ul' in two syllables, not 'sole'.

The honest advice for learners: treat romanization as training wheels with a flat tire. It is inconsistent across books, signs, and names — the same surname appears as Lee, Yi, and Rhee — and it cannot show tense consonants or the ㅓ/ㅡ vowels faithfully. Use it for the first few weeks if you must, then switch to Hangul as fast as you can. Your pronunciation will thank you, because romanization invites you to say English sounds, and Korean sounds are not English sounds.
의 seems to be pronounced three different ways. Is there actually a system to it?

There is, and it is one of Korean's famous pronunciation shape-shifters. The digraph 의 is pronounced differently depending on where it sits:

1. At the start of a word, full value [의]: 의자 (chair), 의사 (doctor), 의미 (meaning).
2. In the middle or end of a word, it usually lightens to [ㅣ]: 회의 (meeting) is [회이], 강의 (lecture) is [강이].
3. As the possessive particle ('of/~'s'), it is pronounced [에]: 우리의 학교 ('our school') is [우리에 학교], and 나의 is [나에].

Why the drift? 의 is articulatorily heavy — a ㅡ gliding into ㅣ — and Korean speakers economize it in unstressed positions, keeping the full form only where it carries a word's identity at the front. The possessive use went furthest because it is a grammatical particle, and particles erode fastest in every language.

For learners: default to [의] at word starts, [ㅣ] elsewhere in words, and [에] when it means possession. Native speakers will understand any of the three almost everywhere; matching the pattern just makes you sound natural.
한국어에는 숫자가 왜 두 가지나 있어요? 언제 어떤 숫자를 써요?

한국어에는 고유어 숫자와 한자어 숫자가 있어요. 고유어 숫자는 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷, 다섯처럼 원래 한국어에서 온 말이고, 한자어 숫자는 일, 이, 삼, 사처럼 한자에서 온 말이에요. 두 체계가 오랫동안 같이 쓰이다 보니, 지금은 상황에 따라 나눠서 써요.

고유어 숫자는 주로 물건을 셀 때와 나이를 말할 때 써요. '사과 세 개', '스물다섯 살'처럼요. 시간에서 '시'를 말할 때도 고유어를 써서 '세 시'라고 해요. 반대로 한자어 숫자는 날짜, 돈, 분, 전화번호에 써요. '삼월 오일', '오천 원', '십 분'처럼요.

한 가지 재미있는 점은 고유어 숫자가 셀 때 모양이 조금 바뀐다는 거예요. 하나는 '한 개', 둘은 '두 개', 셋은 '세 개', 넷은 '네 개'가 돼요. 그리고 고유어 숫자는 마흔, 쉰까지만 일상에서 쓰고 백부터는 한자어를 쓰기 때문에, 큰 숫자는 한자어가 훨씬 편해요.
값 is pronounced 'gap' and 낮 is pronounced 'nat'?? How am I supposed to guess these?

You do not guess — you apply the seven-sound rule. In batchim position, every written consonant is pronounced as one of ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅇ, and the 'flat' letters ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ, ㅎ all collapse to ㄷ. 낮 (daytime) ends in ㅈ, so it is [낟]. 값 (price) ends in ㅄ — a double batchim ㅂ+ㅅ — and before a pause or consonant only the first member sounds: [갑].

Double batchim has its own small logic: before a consonant or at the end of a word, usually only the first consonant is pronounced — 값 is [갑] (the ㅂ of ㅄ sounds) and 몫 (share/portion) is [목] (the ㄱ of ㄳ sounds). But when a vowel follows, both consonants wake up and the second one links: 값을 is [갑쓸] — the ㅅ links and tensifies. 앉다 (to sit) is [안따]: the ㄴㅈ batchim keeps ㄴ, and ㅈ merges with the following ㄷ.

So the system is: single batchim → collapse to seven sounds; double batchim → first one wins before consonants, both appear before vowels. It is a short rule list, and it covers nearly every 'surprise' pronunciation you will meet in your first year.
Is it true a Korean king invented the alphabet because his people couldn't read? That sounds like a legend.

It is documented history, unusually well documented for a writing system. In 1443 (published 1446), King Sejong the Great of Joseon promulgated Hunminjeongeum — 'the correct sounds for teaching the people' — because Classical Chinese characters, the written standard, took years to master and shut common people out of written life. Sejong's own preface says, in essence: because the people's speech differs from Chinese, many cannot express themselves in writing, so he made 28 letters that anyone can learn quickly.

The design is featural, which is rare among the world's scripts: the consonant shapes diagram the speech organs. ㄱ sketches the tongue root blocking the throat, ㄴ the tongue tip at the gum ridge, ㅁ the closed lips, ㅅ the teeth, ㅇ the round throat. Add a stroke and the sound gains aspiration (ㄱ→ㅋ). Vowel letters are built from three elements: a dot/short stroke for heaven, a horizontal line for earth, a vertical line for the human standing between them.

Koreans celebrate this on October 9, Hangul Day. A king commissioning a script specifically so farmers could write letters home is, as far as writing systems go, about as good an origin story as exists — and it happens to be true.
How do the letters physically arrange inside a block? Sometimes the vowel is beside the consonant and sometimes underneath.

The vowel's shape decides the architecture. Korean blocks follow a few fixed layouts:

| Layout | Vowel type | Example | Build |
|---|---|---|---|
| Left + right | tall vowels ㅏ ㅑ ㅓ ㅕ ㅣ | 가 | ㄱ left, ㅏ right |
| Top + bottom | wide vowels ㅗ ㅛ ㅜ ㅠ ㅡ | 구 | ㄱ top, ㅜ below |
| Left + right + bottom | tall vowel + batchim | 한 | ㅎ + ㅏ, ㄴ underneath |
| Top + bottom + bottom | wide vowel + batchim | 글 | ㄱ + ㅡ, ㄹ underneath |

Tall vowels are written vertically, so they stand beside the initial consonant like a partner. Wide vowels are written horizontally, so they lie beneath it like a floor. The batchim, when present, always takes the basement. Compound vowels (ㅘ, ㅙ, ㅝ, ㅞ, ㅢ) wrap around both positions at once, which is why 과 looks fuller than 가.

Once you see blocks as furniture in a fixed room — initial consonant in the main seat, vowel beside or below, batchim in the basement — reading new syllables becomes assembly, not memorization.
같이 is pronounced 'gachi' and 해돋이 is 'haedoji'. Did the ㄷ just turn into ㅈ?

Yes — that is palatalization (구개음화). When a batchim ㄷ or ㅌ is followed by 이 (or a y-glide vowel) across a syllable boundary, it slides forward in the mouth and becomes ㅈ or ㅊ. 같이 (together) is [가치]: the ㅌ of 같 meets 이 and comes out as ㅊ. 해돋이 (sunrise) is [해도지]: the ㄷ links into 이 and palatalizes to ㅈ. 굳이 (insistently) is [구지] the same way.

The mechanics are friendly: ㄷ is made with the tongue tip at the teeth ridge; the vowel 이 pulls the tongue body up toward the hard palate; meet halfway and you land exactly where ㅈ lives. English does the same thing in 'did you' → 'dijoo' and 'got you' → 'gotcha' — Korean just does it systematically and it shows up inside single words, not only across word boundaries.

Practical rule: whenever you see ㄷ/ㅌ batchim followed by 이, expect ㅈ/ㅊ. It also explains spelling-pronunciation gaps in words like 맏이 (eldest child) [마지]. Your tongue was going to do this anyway; Korean phonology simply admits it.
'-네요'와 '-군요'는 어떻게 달라요? 둘 다 놀랄 때 쓰는 것 같은데요.

두 표현 모두 새로 알게 된 사실에 대한 반응을 나타내지만, 느낌이 조금 달라요. '-네요'는 지금 직접 보고 듣고 느끼면서 반응할 때 써요. 비가 오는 창문을 보면서 '비가 오네요'라고 하거나, 음식을 맛보고 '맛있네요'라고 하는 것처럼요. 감탄과 확인이 섞인, 부드럽고 감정적인 반응이에요.

반면에 '-군요'는 정보를 받아들이고 '아, 그렇구나' 하고 이해하거나 확인할 때 더 잘 어울려요. 상대의 말을 듣고 '그렇군요', 소식을 듣고 '벌써 졸업했군요'처럼요. 직접 경험보다는 깨달음의 느낌이 강하고, 조금 더 차분해요.

실제로는 두 표현이 겹치는 상황이 많아서 둘 다 써도 어색하지 않은 경우가 많아요. 다만 '-군요'는 주로 말하는 사람이 혼잣말처럼 확인할 때 자연스럽고, '-네요'는 감정을 담아 반응할 때 자연스러워요. 그리고 '-군요'는 명사 뒤에서는 '-이군요'가 되고, 반말에서는 '-구나'와 '-네'로 짧아져요. '예쁘구나', '예쁘네'처럼요.
Can you walk me through reading 감사합니다 syllable by syllable? I want to see the whole machine work once.

Gladly — 감사합니다 (gam-sa-ham-ni-da, 'thank you', formal) uses almost every rule you know. Five blocks:

감: ㄱ + ㅏ gives 가, batchim ㅁ closes it — 'gam'. 사: ㅅ + ㅏ, no batchim — 'sa'. 합: ㅎ + ㅏ gives 하, batchim ㅂ closes it — 'hap' on paper. 니: ㄴ + ㅣ — 'ni'. 다: ㄷ + ㅏ — 'da'.

Now the spoken form: [감사함니다]. The ㅂ batchim of 합 stands before ㄴ, so nasalization turns ㅂ into ㅁ: 합니다 → [함니다]. Notice nobody changed the spelling — 합니다 keeps the dictionary shape of 하다, and the pronunciation rule adjusts the sound.

That one word is the whole Korean reading story in miniature: assemble blocks mechanically, then let a short list of sound-change rules smooth the joints. If you can read 감사합니다 slowly and correctly, you can read anything in Korean slowly and correctly. Speed is only repetition.
Why does the ㅎ in 좋아요 basically disappear, but in 전화 it turns the next sound into an 'n'?

ㅎ is the weakest consonant in Korean and behaves like a guest who adapts to every room. Between vowels it often fades to almost nothing: 좋아요 is [조아요], 많이 (a lot) is [마니] — the ㅎ is a breath at most. That is intervocalic weakening, and it is why learners mishear 좋아요 as two syllables.

Before or after ㄴ, though, ㅎ does something else: it merges with the nasal. 전화 (telephone) is [저놔] — the ㄴ of 전 pulls the following ㅎ into a second ㄴ. 넣어요 (put in) is [너어요], showing the fade again after a batchim.

And ㅎ has a third life next to stops: 좋다 [조타], where ㅎ fuses with ㄷ into aspirated ㅌ. So ㅎ has three behaviors — fade between vowels, double a neighboring nasal, aspirate a neighboring stop. It sounds chaotic, but each case is just ㅎ being too weak to hold its own shape, so it borrows the shape of whatever stands next to it. Learn the three contexts and ㅎ stops surprising you.
My Korean friend says 개 and 게 sound the same when she says them. Am I deaf, or is she merging them?

She is merging them, and so is nearly every younger speaker in Seoul. ㅐ (ae) and ㅔ (e) were historically distinct — ㅐ more open, ㅔ closer — but in modern standard Korean they have merged for most speakers into a single vowel around [에]. The same merger affects ㅒ and ㅖ. So 개 (dog) and 게 (crab) are homophones in everyday Seoul speech, distinguished by context, and 내가 (I, subject form) vs 네가 (you) is a famous trouble spot — 네가 is often pronounced [니가] precisely to keep it apart from 내가 [내가].

Spelling, however, has not merged. You still must write 개 for dog and 게 for crab, 에 for the particle... no — the location particle is 에, and the difference matters on paper even when ears cannot help you. Learners have to memorize which words take ㅐ and which take ㅔ the way English speakers memorize 'their/there/they're'.

So no, you are not deaf. You are hearing modern Korean accurately; it is the spelling that preserves a distinction the language has mostly retired.
Why does Korean spelling refuse to match pronunciation? 먹다 is spelled with ㄱ even though 먹는 is pronounced with ㅇ in the middle. Wouldn't phonetic spelling be easier?

It would be easier for the first month and harder forever after. Korean spelling is morphophonemic: it spells the meaningful unit, not the sound of the moment. The verb root 먹- (eat) keeps its ㄱ in 먹다, 먹어요, 먹는다, 먹는, even though pronunciation bends it — [먹따], [머거요], [멍는]. Because the spelling holds the root steady, your eye recognizes the same word in every costume, and related words stay visibly related: 깊다 (deep) and 깊이 (deeply) share 깊 even though one is [깁따] and the other [기피].

English quietly does the same thing: 'sign' keeps its silent g because of 'signal'; 'electric' and 'electricity' share a c that sounds different in each. Korean simply applies the principle far more consistently, because Hangul makes it possible — the alphabet could spell phonetically, and Korean orthography deliberately chooses meaning over sound.

The learning consequence is real but manageable: you must learn words in their dictionary spelling and let a finite set of sound rules (linking, nasalization, tensification, aspiration, palatalization) generate the pronunciation. That is a better bargain than it first looks — rules are few, exceptions are rare, and the payoff is that Korean text is remarkably decodable once the rules are yours.
반말은 언제 쓸 수 있어요? 잘못 쓰면 실례가 된다고 들었어요.

반말은 아주 가까운 사이에서만 쓸 수 있는 말투예요. 보통 오랜 친구, 나이가 같은 동료, 어린 동생이나 아이에게 써요. 처음 만난 사람이나 나이가 많은 사람, 직장 상사에게 반말을 쓰면 큰 실례가 돼요. 한국에서는 나이와 관계가 말투를 결정하기 때문에, 반말은 '우리가 이만큼 가깝다'는 신호이기도 해요.

그래서 한국 사람들은 사이가 가까워지면 '말을 놓자'고 제안하기도 해요. 한쪽이 먼저 제안하고 서로 동의했을 때 반말로 바꾸는 것이 자연스러워요. 반대로 상대가 반말을 쓴다고 해서 나도 바로 반말을 써도 되는 것은 아니에요. 나이 차이가 있으면 더 조심해야 해요.

외국인이라면 존댓말부터 익히는 것이 안전해요. 실수로 반말을 써도 외국인이니까 이해해 주는 경우가 많지만, 존댓말을 쓰면 언제나 좋은 인상을 줘요. 반말은 드라마에서 많이 들리지만, 그건 가까운 관계의 대화라는 점을 기억하세요. 친해지고 싶은 사람이 생기면, 그 사람이 먼저 말을 놓자고 할 때까지 기다리는 것이 좋아요.
밤 means both 'night' and 'chestnut', and 눈 means both 'snow' and 'eye'. Is Korean just full of homophones?

It has plenty, and you have found two of the classics. 눈 오는 밤 — 'a snowy night' — uses both words in their weather senses, and a sentence like 눈에 눈이 들어갔어요 ('something got in my eye', literally 'an eye entered the eye' if the first 눈 is read wrong) shows the chaos potential. In older Korean, 밤 (night) and 밤 (chestnut) differed in vowel length, and 눈 (snow) and 눈 (eye) did too; modern Seoul Korean has mostly dropped vowel length, merging the pairs.

Korean copes the way all languages cope: context, particles, and collocations. 눈에 is almost always the eye (snow does not take the location-of-body reading), 눈이 와요 is always snow because eyes do not fall from the sky, and 밤에 만나요 is a meeting at night, not a meeting at a chestnut.

Korean also imports disambiguation through its Sino-Korean vocabulary: when precision matters, 밤 gets specified as 야간 (nighttime hours) or 밤하늘 (night sky), and 눈 as 눈동자 (pupil/eyeball region) in careful usage. For learners, the lesson is reassuring: homophones look terrifying in a dictionary list and almost never cause trouble in a real sentence, because grammar marks which world you are in.
Everyone says 은/는 is 'topic' and 이/가 is 'subject', but that doesn't help me choose. Give me something that actually works.

Use this working rule: 은/는 presents old, shared information — 'as for X' — while 이/가 presents new or singled-out information — 'it is X (that...)'. Compare: 저는 학생이에요 ('As for me, I'm a student' — introducing yourself, topic). 누가 왔어요? 철수가 왔어요 ('Who came? Cheolsu came' — the answer is new information, so 이/가). You cannot answer 누가 with 는: 철수는 왔어요 would sound like 'As for Cheolsu (never mind the others), he came'.

A second test: 이/가 is used for first mention, 은/는 for what has already entered the conversation. 옛날에 한 남자가 살았어요. 그 남자는... ('Once a man lived. The man...') — first appearance takes 가, later references take 는.

And a third: descriptive sentences about a specific observed thing take 이/가 — 날씨가 좋아요 ('The weather is good', commenting on today's weather as news), while general truths take 은/는 — 겨울은 추워요 ('Winter is cold'). When in doubt: brand-new or answering 'who/what' → 이/가; already on the table or making a general statement → 은/는.
My tutor corrected '저는 할게요' to '제가 할게요' when I volunteered to do something. Why is 가 better there?

Because volunteering singles you out, and singling out is 이/가's home turf. 제가 할게요 means 'I (as opposed to anyone else) will do it' — the 가 focuses the subject as the selected one. 저는 할게요 is not wrong, but it frames you as the topic ('as for me, I'll do it'), which sounds more like stating your plans than stepping forward. In a room where someone asks 누가 할래요? ('Who wants to do it?'), the natural answer is 제가 할게요.

This is the exhaustive-listing force of 이/가: it points at one member of a set and excludes the rest. The same logic runs 누가 왔어요? — 민수가 왔어요 (it was Minsu who came), and 이거 누가 만들었어요? — 제가 만들었어요.

Watch for it in negations and emphasis too: 네가 가야 해 ('YOU have to go' — not me), and in the classic 제가 커피를 살게요 ('I'll buy the coffee' — my treat, my move). Whenever the unspoken question is 'who, specifically?', reach for 이/가, and for pronouns that means 제가, 네가, 누가 rather than 저는, 너는.
'은/는'과 '이/가'의 차이를 한국어로 쉽게 설명해 주세요.

'은/는'은 이야기의 주제를 정하는 조사이고, '이/가'는 새로운 정보를 알려 주는 조사예요. 쉽게 말하면 '은/는'은 '말하자면'이라는 느낌이고, '이/가'는 '바로 이거'라는 느낌이에요.

예를 들어 자기소개를 할 때는 '저는 학생이에요'라고 해요. '저'라는 주제를 꺼내 놓고 설명하는 거예요. 그런데 '누가 왔어요?'라는 질문에는 '민수가 왔어요'라고 대답해요. 누가 왔는지가 새로운 정보라서 '가'를 쓰는 거예요. 여기에 '민수는 왔어요'라고 하면 '민수 말인데, 오기는 왔어요' 같은 뉘앙스가 돼서 대답으로는 어색해요.

또 처음 나오는 대상에는 '이/가'를 쓰고, 이미 나온 대상에는 '은/는'을 써요. '옛날에 한 남자가 살았어요. 그 남자는 마음이 착했어요'처럼요. 그리고 일반적인 사실을 말할 때는 '은/는'이 자연스러워요. '겨울은 추워요'처럼요. 반대로 지금 눈앞의 상황을 전할 때는 '날씨가 좋아요'처럼 '이/가'를 써요. 새로운 정보인지, 이미 아는 주제인지를 생각하면 고르기 쉬워요.
How do I know whether to use 을 or 를? And does it matter if I get it wrong?

The rule is mechanical and total: if the noun ends in a batchim (final consonant), use 을; if it ends in a vowel, use 를. 책을 읽어요 ('read a book' — 책 ends in ㄱ), 사과를 먹어요 ('eat an apple' — 사과 ends in a vowel), 물을 마셔요, 커피를 마셔요. There are no exceptions and no irregular nouns; if you can hear whether the word ends in a consonant or a vowel, you can choose correctly every time.

Does it matter? For understanding, barely — 을/를 only marks the object, and word order plus context usually carry the meaning anyway, so a mistake will not confuse anyone. For sounding natural, yes, it matters a lot, because natives choose instantly and an error is conspicuous, like saying 'a apple' in English. The good news: this is the easiest particle pair in Korean precisely because it is 100% phonological.

While you are here, note the spoken shortcut: in fast casual speech, 을/를 is often dropped entirely when the object is obvious — 밥 먹었어요? ('Have you eaten?') — but learners should keep it until their instincts are native-grade.
에 and 에서 both seem to mean 'at/in'. When do I use which one?

Ask whether anything is happening there. 에 marks a static point — existence, destination, or time. 에서 marks the stage where an action unfolds.

에: 집에 있어요 ('I'm at home' — just being there), 책이 책상 위에 있어요 (existence/location), 학교에 가요 ('go to school' — destination), 세 시에 만나요 ('meet at 3' — time point).

에서: 학교에서 공부해요 ('I study at school' — studying happens there), 공원에서 운동해요 ('exercise in the park'), 도서관에서 친구를 만났어요 ('met a friend at the library').

The classic minimal pair: 집에 있어요 (I am at home) vs 집에서 자요 (I sleep at home). Same place, different particle, because sleeping is an action and being is not. Verbs of existence (있다, 없다, 살다 in its 'reside' sense) take 에; action verbs take 에서.

One more 에서 job: marking where something comes from — 미국에서 왔어요 ('I came from America'). English collapses 'at' and 'from' contexts that Korean keeps apart, so let the verb decide: action happening → 에서; just located or heading to → 에.
Do I put 에 after every time expression? 'Tomorrow at' feels like it should need one.

No — and this is a place where Korean is more relaxed than English. 에 attaches to clock times and calendar points: 세 시에 (at 3 o'clock), 월요일에 (on Monday), 주말에 (on the weekend), 2027년에 (in 2027), 아침에 (in the morning).

But a small set of time words refuses 에 entirely: 오늘 (today), 어제 (yesterday), 내일 (tomorrow), 모레 (the day after tomorrow), 지금 (now), 언제 (when). You say 내일 가요, never 내일에 가요. These words are already adverbial — they behave like English 'today' and 'tomorrow', which also reject 'on' and 'at'.

A useful parallel: English says 'at 3', 'on Monday', 'in the morning' but bare 'tomorrow'. Korean says 세 시에, 월요일에, 아침에 but bare 내일. The logic matches almost exactly — specific points on the clock or calendar get a marker, relative day-words stand alone.

Edge case: 매일 (every day), 작년 (last year), 다음 주 (next week) also stand bare. When in doubt, ask whether the word names a point you could circle on a calendar or clock — if yes, 에; if it is a relative 'when' word, leave it bare.
에게, 한테, 께 — three ways to say 'to someone'? When does each one appear?

All three mark the recipient of giving, telling, or sending, and they divide by politeness and medium. 한테 is the everyday spoken form: 친구한테 말했어요 ('I told my friend'), 동생한테 줬어요. 에게 is its more written, formal twin: 학생에게 공지했어요 ('notified the students') — you will see 에게 in announcements, essays, and news, and hear 한테 in conversation.

께 is the honorific form, used when the recipient is someone you elevate: 선생님께 드렸어요 ('I gave it to my teacher'), 할머니께 여쭤봤어요 ('I asked Grandmother'). Notice 께 pairs with honorific verbs like 드리다 and 여쭙다 — the whole phrase rises together.

Two traps. First, these particles attach to people and animals, not things: you send a package 서울에 (to Seoul, place marker 에), not 서울에게. Second, the 'from' counterparts exist: 한테서/에게서 mean 'from someone' — 친구한테서 들었어요 ('I heard it from a friend').

Rule of thumb: speaking to friends about friends → 한테; writing → 에게; recipient deserves honor → 께. Mixing 한테 with a respected elder is the kind of small error that marks a learner instantly, so let 께 become automatic for teachers, grandparents, and clients.
'에'와 '에서'는 어떻게 구분해서 써요? 예를 들어서 알려 주세요.

구분하는 방법은 간단해요. 그 장소에서 어떤 행동이 일어나는지를 생각하면 돼요. 그냥 있거나, 도착하거나, 시간의 지점을 말할 때는 '에'를 써요. 반대로 공부하거나 운동하는 것처럼 동작이 일어나는 장소에는 '에서'를 써요.

예를 들어 '집에 있어요'는 집이라는 장소에 존재한다는 뜻이라서 '에'를 써요. 그런데 '집에서 공부해요'는 집에서 공부라는 행동이 일어나니까 '에서'를 써요. '학교에 가요'도 도착하는 곳을 말하니까 '에'이고, '학교에서 점심을 먹어요'는 먹는 행동이 일어나니까 '에서'예요.

'에서'에는 또 하나의 뜻이 있어요. 출발점을 나타내서 '미국에서 왔어요'처럼 '부터'의 의미로도 써요.

정리하면, 있다/없다처럼 존재를 나타내거나 가는 목적지, 그리고 시간을 말할 때는 '에', 동작이 벌어지는 장소와 출발점에는 '에서'를 쓰면 돼요. 동사가 동작 동사인지가 가장 확실한 기준이에요.
사과와 배, 사과하고 배, 사과랑 배 — are 와/과, 하고, and (이)랑 all just 'and'?

They all mean 'and/with', and the difference is pure register — who you are talking to, not what you mean. 와/과 is the neutral-to-formal written choice: 사과와 배, 회의와 보고. The form still depends on batchim: vowel-ending nouns take 와 (사과와), batchim nouns take 과 (책과 연필).

하고 is the all-purpose spoken form: 사과하고 배, 친구하고 놀았어요 ('played with a friend'). It is safe in nearly all conversation. (이)랑 is the casual, friendly form: vowel nouns take 랑 (사과랑), batchim nouns take 이랑 (책이랑), and it lives in relaxed speech — 친구랑 영화 봤어요.

Think of it as English 'and' vs a written 'together with' vs a casual ''n''. Meaning never changes; texture does. A learner who uses 하고 everywhere in speech will sound perfectly natural, and 와/과 is what you want in essays and presentations.

One bonus use: 와/과 and 하고 also mean 'with' for companionship — 누구랑 갔어요? ('Who did you go with?'). Korean does not separate 'and' from 'with' here the way English does, which actually makes life easier.
What do 도 and 만 do? They seem tiny but they're everywhere.

도 means 'also/too/even' and it replaces the particle that would otherwise be there: 저도 가요 ('I'm going too' — 도 replaces 는), 커피도 주세요 ('coffee too, please' — replaces 를), 서울에도 눈이 와요 ('it's snowing in Seoul too' — stacks after 에, one of the few particles 도 follows rather than replaces).

만 means 'only' and it limits: 이것만 주세요 ('just this one, please'), 세 개만 샀어요 ('I bought only three'), 한국어로만 말해요 ('speak only in Korean'). It also replaces subject/object particles: 저만 몰랐어요 ('only I didn't know').

Together they form a useful pair: 도 opens the set wider, 만 narrows it to one. Korean even combines them: 이것도 저것도 다 좋아요 ('this too and that too — I like them all').

A listening tip: 도 often carries the emotional weight of a sentence — 저도요 ('me too!') is one of the most common reactions in Korean conversation, and 나도 몰라 ('I don't know either') sounds very different from 나는 몰라. Small particles, big feelings: worth learning early.
How does (으)로 work? I've seen it mean 'by bus', 'to Seoul', and 'with a pencil' — that can't all be one particle.

It is one particle with a family of related meanings: direction, means, and material — all loosely 'by way of'. 버스로 가요 ('go by bus' — means), 서울로 가요 ('head to Seoul' — direction), 연필로 써요 ('write with a pencil' — instrument), 한국어로 말해요 ('speak in Korean' — medium), 나무로 만들었어요 ('made of wood' — material). The shared thread: 로 marks the path or channel through which something happens.

Choosing the form: after a vowel or a ㄹ batchim, use 로 (버스로, 서울로, 연필로 — 연필 ends in ㄹ, so it takes 로); after any other batchim, use 으로 (집으로, 부산으로, 책으로).

Direction 로 vs 에: 학교에 가요 states the destination neutrally; 학교로 가요 emphasizes heading in that direction, and is the form in set phrases like 집으로 돌아가요. For learners, 에 is the safe default for destinations, and 로 is your tool for transport, tools, and language-of-speech.

Also note 로 in choices and roles: 대표로 뽑혔어요 ('was chosen as the representative'). Same particle, 'in the capacity of' — still the channel idea.
부터 and 까지 — do they only work with time, or with places too?

Both. 부터 marks the starting point and 까지 the end point, for time, place, and even quantities. Time: 월요일부터 금요일까지 일해요 ('work from Monday to Friday'), 아침부터 밤까지 공부했어요 ('studied from morning till night'). Place: 집에서 학교까지 걸어요 ('walk from home to school') — note place-부터 usually pairs with 에서 for the start point, though 서울부터 부산까지 ('from Seoul to Busan') is fine too. Quantity: 열 개까지 살 수 있어요 ('can buy up to ten').

까지 has an extra flavor 부터 lacks: 'even/unexpectedly'. 너까지 왔어? ('even you came?'), 비까지 와요 ('it's even raining'). Context makes it clear.

A very common learner pattern: 처음부터 끝까지 ('from beginning to end') — you will hear it in instructions, stories, and complaints alike.

Word order caution: the 부터 phrase comes before the 까지 phrase, and both come before the verb, as Korean modifiers always do. 아침부터 밤까지 일했어요 is the natural frame; build your sentence inside it.
'-아서'와 '-니까'의 차이는 무엇인가요? 이유를 말하는 표현인 건 알겠는데요.

둘 다 이유를 나타내지만, 쓸 수 있는 상황이 달라요. 가장 큰 차이는 뒤에 오는 문장이에요. '-니까' 뒤에는 명령이나 제안이 올 수 있지만, '-아서' 뒤에는 올 수 없어요. 예를 들어 '비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요'는 자연스럽지만, '비가 와서 우산을 가져가세요'는 어색해요. 청유문 '같이 가요'도 '-니까'와만 어울려요.

뉘앙스도 조금 달라요. '-아서'는 원인과 결과가 자연스럽게 이어질 때, 그리고 결과를 말하는 사람이 직접 겪은 일일 때 잘 어울려요. '늦어서 죄송합니다', '만나서 반갑습니다'처럼 인사말에도 많이 써요. 반면에 '-니까'는 말하는 사람이 판단한 이유를 내세우는 느낌이 강해서, 설명하거나 설득할 때 자주 써요.

형태에서도 차이가 있어요. '-아서'는 동사의 어간 끝 모음에 따라 '-아서'와 '-어서'로 나뉘고, 과거 시제와 함께 쓰지 않아요. '비가 왔어서'가 아니라 '비가 와서'라고 해요. '-니까'는 '비가 왔으니까'처럼 과거형과도 함께 쓸 수 있어요. 정리하면, 뒤에 명령이나 제안이 오면 무조건 '-니까', 부드러운 인과 관계면 '-아서'가 안전해요.
Why can I say 비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요 but not 비가 와서 우산을 가져가세요? Both mean 'because it's raining'.

Because -니까 and -아서 divide the 'because' world by what kind of sentence may follow. -니까 presents a reason as the speaker's judgment — a premise for a decision — so it freely precedes commands, suggestions, and questions: 비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요 ('Since it's raining, take an umbrella'), 추우니까 창문을 닫을까요? ('Since it's cold, shall we close the window?').

-아서/-어서 expresses a natural cause-and-effect flow, usually about events rather than decisions, and it refuses commands and suggestions. 비가 와서 우산을 가져가세요 breaks because 'take an umbrella' is your decision, not rain's natural result. 비가 와서 경기가 취소됐어요 ('The match was cancelled because of rain') is perfect — an outcome, not an order.

Two more -아서 traits: it cannot carry past tense on the reason clause (비가 와서, not 왔어서), and it lives in set greetings: 만나서 반갑습니다 ('nice to meet you' — literally 'because we met, I'm glad'), 늦어서 죄송합니다 ('sorry for being late').

Memory rule: telling someone what to do? The reason needs -니까. Reporting what happened? -아서 flows.
How do I choose between 았 and 었 for the past tense? 가다 becomes 갔어요 but 먹다 becomes 먹었어요.

Look at the last vowel of the verb stem. If it is ㅏ or ㅗ, use 았; for every other vowel, use 었. 가다 (ㅏ) → 갔어요, 오다 (ㅗ) → 왔어요, 좋다 (ㅗ) → 좋았어요. 먹다 (ㅓ) → 먹었어요, 읽다 (ㅡ) → 읽었어요, 배우다 (ㅜ) → 배웠어요.

Then contraction does its work: stem vowel + 았/었 usually fuses into one syllable. 가 + 았어요 → 갔어요, 오 + 았어요 → 왔어요, 보 + 았어요 → 봤어요, 주 + 었어요 → 줬어요, 마시 + 었어요 → 마셨어요. 하다 is its own world: 했어요, and every -하다 verb follows (공부했어요, 일했어요).

A few stems end in vowels that swallow the marker: 되다 → 됐어요, 서다 → 섰어요.

Practical approach: learn each new verb together with its past form as a pair — 가다/갔어요, 먹다/먹었어요 — the way English learners learn go/went. The vowel rule explains the pattern afterward and predicts new verbs reliably, but the contracted forms need to become reflexes, and pairs make reflexes.
Why is 'hot' 더워요 and not 덥어요? And 'easy' is 쉬워요? These ㅂ verbs keep ambushing me.

Welcome to the ㅂ-irregular family, one of Korean's small, learnable ambushes. When a stem ends in ㅂ and meets a vowel-initial ending, the ㅂ drops and 우 (often surfacing as 워) moves in: 덥다 → 더워요, 춥다 → 추워요, 맵다 → 매워요, 어렵다 → 어려워요, 쉽다 → 쉬워요, 가깝다 → 가까워요, 무겁다 → 무거워요. So 덥 + 어요 becomes 더워요 by way of 덥 → 더우 + 어요 → 더워요.

Most of these are descriptive verbs (adjectives) for weather, taste, weight, and difficulty — a coherent little clan worth memorizing as a set.

But not every ㅂ stem joins: 입다 (to wear) → 입어요, 잡다 (to catch) → 잡아요, 좁다 (narrow) → 좁아요. These stay regular. How to tell? The irregulars are mostly the common descriptive words; the safe strategy is to memorize the famous irregular set (덥다, 춥다, 맵다, 쉽다, 어렵다, 가깝다, 무겁다, 가볍다, 아름답다, 고맙다 — 감사's cousin 고맙다 → 고마워요) and treat action verbs in ㅂ as regular unless told otherwise.

Bonus: the same change hits nouns forms — 더위 (the heat), 추위 (the cold) — so the family pays rent beyond one conjugation.
듣다 becomes 들어요, 모르다 becomes 몰라요, 크다 becomes 커요. Is there any pattern here or do I just memorize?

There are three small patterns hiding in your three examples, and each covers a family.

ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 (listen) → 들어요, 걷다 (walk) → 걸어요, 묻다 (ask) → 물어요, 싣다 (load) → 실어요. When these ㄷ-final stems meet a vowel ending, ㄷ becomes ㄹ. The irregular set is just those few common verbs; most ㄷ verbs are regular — 받다 → 받아요, 믿다 → 믿어요, 닫다 → 닫아요. One spelling trap: 묻다 'to ask' is irregular (물어요), but 묻다 'to bury' is regular (묻어요) — same spelling, different verb, different behavior.

르-irregular: 모르다 (not know) → 몰라요, 부르다 (call/sing) → 불러요, 빠르다 (fast) → 빨라요. The 르 doubles: stem + ㄹ + the vowel ending, choosing 아/어 by the preceding vowel — 몰라 (ㅗ → 아), 불러 (ㅜ → 어).

ㅡ-irregular: 크다 (big) → 커요, 쓰다 (write) → 써요, 바쁘다 (busy) → 바빠요. The ㅡ drops and the ending vowel copies the previous syllable's harmony: 크 → 커 (ㅓ family), 바쁘 → 바빠 (ㅏ family).

So: memorize three rules and three small word lists, not hundreds of forms. Korean irregulars are irregular in formation but perfectly regular in behavior once you know the family.
과거형에서 '-았-'과 '-었-'은 어떻게 골라요?

동사 어간의 마지막 모음을 보면 돼요. 마지막 모음이 'ㅏ'나 'ㅗ'이면 '-았-'을 쓰고, 그 밖의 모음이면 '-었-'을 써요. 예를 들어 '가다'는 ㅏ로 끝나니까 '갔어요'가 되고, '오다'는 ㅗ로 끝나니까 '왔어요'가 돼요. 반대로 '먹다'는 ㅓ로 끝나서 '먹었어요', '읽다'는 ㅡ로 끝나서 '읽었어요'가 돼요.

실제로 말할 때는 모음이 합쳐지는 경우가 많아요. '보'와 '았어요'가 만나면 '봤어요'가 되고, '주'와 '었어요'가 만나면 '줬어요'가 돼요. 그리고 '하다'는 특별해서 '했어요'가 되고, '공부하다, 일하다' 같은 말도 모두 '공부했어요, 일했어요'처럼 똑같이 바뀌어요.

헷갈릴 때는 마지막 모음만 확인하세요. ㅏ와 ㅗ는 밝은 모음이라 '-았-'과 어울리고, 나머지는 '-었-'과 어울려요. 이 규칙 하나면 대부분의 동사 과거형을 만들 수 있어요. 다만 '덥다'가 '더웠어요'가 되는 것처럼 받침이 바뀌는 불규칙 동사는 따로 외워야 해요.
I know -고 is 'and' for verbs. What do -지만 and -는데 add that -고 doesn't?

Three connectors, three relationships. -고 is pure addition: 밥을 먹고 잤어요 ('I ate and slept') — sequence or list, no comment on how the parts relate. -지만 is direct contrast, 'but': 비싸지만 맛있어요 ('It's expensive but delicious'), 작지만 편해요 ('small but comfortable'). Use it when the second half pushes against the first.

-는데 is the subtle one. It sets a background scene or a soft contrast, and often leaves the sentence hanging as an invitation: 밖에 비가 오는데 우산 있어요? ('It's raining outside — do you have an umbrella?'), 저는 학생인데요 ('I'm a student, and...' — said while expecting the listener to respond, very common when introducing a request). As a mid-sentence connector it can be contrast ('좋아하는데 비싸요' — I like it, but it's pricey) or background ('집에 갔는데 아무도 없었어요' — I went home and/but nobody was there).

The beginner's map: sequence → -고, hard 'but' → -지만, scene-setting or soft pivot → -는데. The -는데요 ending deserves special attention because Koreans constantly end utterances with it to sound gentle and open-ended; translating it word-for-word fails, but hearing it as 'here's my situation...' works.
Why do I say 가고 싶어요 for myself but 가고 싶어해요 about my sister? 싶다 changes?

싶다 is a 'mind-reading restricted' verb. Korean grammar treats direct statements about inner states — wanting, being glad, being sick in the felt sense — as things you can only assert about yourself. For your own desire: 저는 한국에 가고 싶어요 ('I want to go to Korea'), 엄마가 보고 싶어요 ('I miss Mom').

For a third person, you must report observable signs instead, and the language adds -어하다 to make that report form: 동생은 한국에 가고 싶어해요 ('My younger sibling wants to go' — as shown by what she says and does). Same pattern with 좋아요 → 좋아해요 for others' feelings in careful speech, and 아파요 → 아파해요.

Questions flip the rule: to ask about the listener's feelings, plain 싶어요 is right — 커피 마시고 싶어요? ('Do you want coffee?') — because you are asking the one person who can know.

This is not pedantry; saying 엄마는 가고 싶어요 marks you as a learner instantly. The deeper pattern is worth noticing: Korean grammar encodes epistemic humility — you state your own heart directly and everyone else's only as evidence. Several verb families (feelings, desires, sensations) share this split.
안 가요, 못 가요, 가지 않아요, 가지 못해요 — four ways to not go. What's the map?

Two axes: which negative, and short or long form. 안 is plain negation — 'don't/doesn't': 안 가요 ('I'm not going'), 안 먹어요, 안 비싸요 ('not expensive'). 못 is inability — 'can't': 못 가요 ('I can't go' — something prevents me), 수영을 못 해요 ('I can't swim'). The difference matters socially: 회의에 안 가요 says you're skipping the meeting; 회의에 못 가요 says you're unable to attend — the second is the polite excuse, the first can sound defiant.

The long forms put the negative at the end with -지: 가지 않아요 ('do not go' — softer, more written or careful), 가지 못해요 ('cannot go'). Long forms sound slightly more formal and are common in announcements and careful speech: 운영하지 않습니다 ('not in operation').

Placement note: 안 and 못 sit before the verb, but with -하다 verbs they split the noun and 하다: 공부를 안 해요 ('don't study'), 공부를 못 해요 ('can't study'). And prohibition is its own form entirely: 가지 마세요 ('please don't go') — never 안 with a command.

Quick map: choice/fact → 안; blocked ability → 못; careful/written → -지 않다/-지 못하다; telling someone not to → -지 마세요.
좋다 takes 이/가 but 좋아하다 takes 을/를, even though both translate as 'like'. What's going on?

They are different parts of speech wearing similar clothes. 좋다 is a descriptive verb (adjective): 'to be good/likable'. The thing evaluated is the subject, so it takes 이/가: 날씨가 좋아요 ('The weather is good'), 저는 이 노래가 좋아요 ('I like this song' — literally 'this song is good to me'). 좋아하다 is an action verb: 'to like, to be fond of' — an activity your heart performs on an object, so the object takes 을/를: 저는 이 노래를 좋아해요, 커피를 좋아해요.

The meanings overlap but the framing differs, and natives feel it: 이 커피가 좋아요 evaluates the coffee; 이 커피를 좋아해요 states your fondness. Both are correct and common; the 가 version often sounds like a reaction in the moment, the 를 version like a standing preference.

The pattern generalizes to a family of 'emotion adjectives' that take 이/가 where English expects an object: 무서워요 in 이 영화가 무서워요 ('this movie is scary/I find it scary'), 필요해요 in 돈이 필요해요 ('I need money' — 'money is necessary'), 보고 싶어요 in 엄마가 보고 싶어요 ('I miss Mom').

Learner trap: 저는 커피가 좋아해요 is fine, but 저는 커피를 좋아요 is broken — 를 demands the verb 좋아하다. Match the particle to the verb's grammar, not to the English translation, and this whole family falls into place.
'좋다'와 '좋아하다'는 왜 조사까지 달라요? 둘 다 'like' 아닌가요?

영어로는 둘 다 'like'로 번역되지만, 한국어에서는 품사가 달라요. '좋다'는 형용사라서 주어를 설명하는 말이에요. 그래서 주어 조사 '이/가'를 써요. '날씨가 좋아요'는 날씨가 좋다는 뜻이고, '저는 이 노래가 좋아요'도 노래가 좋다고 평가하는 거예요.

반면에 '좋아하다'는 동사예요. 마음이 대상을 향해서 움직이는 동작이라서, 목적어 조사 '을/를'을 써요. '저는 이 노래를 좋아해요', '커피를 좋아해요'처럼요.

그래서 '저는 커피를 좋아요'라고 하면 틀린 문장이 돼요. '를'을 썼으면 동사인 '좋아하다'가 와야 하고, '좋다'를 쓰려면 '커피가 좋아요'가 되어야 해요.

이런 패턴은 다른 감정 표현에도 나타나요. '돈이 필요해요', '이 영화가 무서워요', '엄마가 보고 싶어요'처럼, 영어로는 목적어 자리에 올 것 같은 대상이 한국어에서는 주어가 되는 경우가 많아요. 조사는 영어 뜻이 아니라 한국어 동사의 성격에 맞춰 고른다고 생각하면 이해하기 쉬워요.
How do Korean relative clauses work? 'The book I bought yesterday' — where does everything go?

Korean puts the whole describing clause before the noun, with a special ending glued to the verb, and there are no relative pronouns — no 'that/who/which'. The ending depends on tense: past -(으)ㄴ, present -는, future -(으)ㄹ.

Past: 어제 산 책 ('the book I bought yesterday' — 사다 + ㄴ), 제가 읽은 책 ('the book I read'). Present: 지금 읽는 책 ('the book I'm reading now'), 한국어를 가르치는 선생님 ('the teacher who teaches Korean'). Future: 내일 갈 곳 ('the place I'll go tomorrow'), 다음에 만날 사람 ('the person I'll meet next').

With descriptive verbs (adjectives), present state uses -(으)ㄴ: 큰 집 ('a big house'), 예쁜 꽃 ('a pretty flower'), and past/completed uses -던 or 았던: 어제 더웠던 날씨 ('the weather that was hot yesterday').

Everything English puts after the noun, Korean stacks before it, and the stack can grow: 어제 도서관에서 친구가 추천한 책 ('the book my friend recommended at the library yesterday') — one long modifier, then 책. Build the habit of finishing the description before naming the thing, and Korean sentences stop feeling backwards; they are just front-loaded.
How do I say 'before' and 'after' with verbs in Korean? Like 'before sleeping' or 'after class ends'.

Three frames cover almost everything. For 'when': -(으)ㄹ 때 — 밥을 먹을 때 ('when eating'), 어렸을 때 ('when I was young'), 바쁠 때 ('when busy'). 때 is a noun meaning 'time', and the verb before it wears the future-looking ㄹ ending because the moment is viewed as a point.

For 'before': -기 전에 — 자기 전에 양치해요 ('brush my teeth before sleeping'), 떠나기 전에 전화하세요 ('call before you leave'). 전에 means 'in front of/before', and the verb takes the plain nominalizer -기. A fixed treasure: 식사 전에 손을 씻으세요 ('wash your hands before meals').

For 'after': -(으)ㄴ 후에 or -고 나서 — 수업이 끝난 후에 만나요 ('let's meet after class ends'), 밥을 먹은 후에 산책해요. 후에 is 'after' as a noun, and the verb takes the past-style ㄴ because the first event must be complete. The -고 나서 variant (먹고 나서) sounds a touch more spoken and sequential.

Notice the logic of the endings: before-events use the un-realized form (기/ㄹ), after-events use the completed form (ㄴ). Korean marks the timeline inside the grammar, not just with the words 전에/후에.
Korean has multiple levels of politeness. How many do I actually need, and which one should be my default?

Three levels cover real life. 해요체 (the -아요/어요 style) is the default: polite, warm, and safe with strangers, coworkers, shop staff, and new acquaintances — 가요, 먹어요, 좋아요. Learn this first and use it 90% of the time. 합쇼체/합니다체 (the -입니다/-합니다 style) is formal: presentations, news, military, ceremonies, and first-business-meeting Korean — 갑니다, 먹습니다, 좋습니다. It sounds stiff in cafés but correct in boardrooms.

해체, better known as 반말 ('half speech'), is the intimate/plain level for close friends, family, and children: 가, 먹어, 좋아. Using it upward — to elders or strangers — is a genuine social offense, not a grammar slip.

There are historical and middle levels (하오체, 하게체) that you will meet in period dramas and from some older speakers, but you only need to recognize them, not produce them.

The strategic point: politeness in Korean is not decoration added to a sentence; it is baked into the verb ending of every sentence. You cannot say a 'neutral' Korean sentence — you always choose a stance toward your listener. Default to 해요체 and let relationships, not vocabulary lists, tell you when to move.
How is 해요체 built? I want the mechanics, not just examples.

해요체 is the polite informal style, and its engine is the -아/어 vowel ending plus 요. Choose the ending by the stem's last vowel: ㅏ/ㅗ stems take 아 (가다 → 가요, 보다 → 봐요), all others take 어 (먹다 → 먹어요, 읽다 → 읽어요), and 하다 verbs take 해요 (공부하다 → 공부해요) — which is where the style gets its name.

Contractions smooth the results: 오 + 아요 → 와요, 주 + 어요 → 줘요, 마시 + 어요 → 마셔요, 되 + 어요 → 돼요. Descriptive verbs use the identical machinery: 좋아요, 바빠요, 커요.

Questions need nothing extra — raise your intonation: 가요? 먹어요? Statements, questions, and soft suggestions all wear the same form, differentiated by melody and context, which is part of why 해요체 feels conversational.

Commands get their own polite form, -(으)세요: 앉으세요 ('please sit'), 천천히 하세요 ('take your time'). Prohibition is -지 마세요: 만지지 마세요 ('please don't touch').

Build order for learners: master statement/question 해요체 first, then -(으)세요 requests. That pair handles nearly every service encounter, friendship, and workplace conversation you will have in your first years.
한국어의 존댓말은 왜 영어보다 복잡한가요?

영어에서는 상대가 누구든 대부분 같은 문장을 쓰지만, 한국어에서는 문장을 끝낼 때마다 상대와의 관계를 골라야 하기 때문이에요. 친구에게는 '가', 어른에게는 '가요', 공식적인 자리에서는 '갑니다'라고 하듯이, 동사의 끝이 상대에 대한 태도를 나타내요. 존댓말을 안 쓰는 선택지가 거의 없다는 것이 영어와 가장 다른 점이에요.

복잡한 이유는 존댓말이 한 가지가 아니라 여러 층으로 이루어져 있기 때문이에요. 첫째, 문장 끝의 말투가 달라져요. 둘째, 주어를 높이는 '-시-'가 들어가요. '할아버지께서 오셨어요'처럼요. 셋째, 단어 자체가 바뀌기도 해요. '먹다'는 '드시다'가 되고, '자다'는 '주무시다'가 돼요. 넷째, 자기 자신을 낮추는 말도 있어요. '나'는 '저'가 되고, '주다'는 '드리다'가 돼요.

이런 체계가 생긴 것은 나이에 따라 위아래를 구분하는 문화와 깊은 관련이 있어요. 하지만 복잡한 만큼 표현도 풍부해요. 말투 하나로 거리감, 존경, 친근함을 모두 조절할 수 있으니까요. 외국인 학습자는 해요체부터 익히면 대부분의 상황에서 안전하게 말할 수 있어요.
What does the -시- in 오셨어요 actually do? It seems to appear whenever grandparents are involved.

-시- (expanded as -으시- after consonants) is the subject-honorific marker: it raises the person doing the action. 오셨어요 = 오 (come) + 시 (honor) + 었 (past) + 어요 (polite ending) — 'Grandmother came', with the grammar itself bowing to Grandmother. 선생님이 말씀하세요 ('the teacher speaks'), 아버지가 읽으세요 ('Father reads'), 할머니가 웃으셨어요 ('Grandmother smiled').

It pairs with the subject particle 께서: 할아버지께서 주무세요. And it only honors the subject of the sentence — never you, the speaker, and never a random object. Saying 제가 가시... would be a classic error: you cannot honor yourself.

Note the double politeness layers in a sentence like 할머니께서 오셨어요: 께서 honors her as subject, -시- honors her action, and -어요 honors you, the listener. Korean politeness works on two independent axes — respect for the person talked about, and politeness toward the person talked to — and -시- belongs to the first axis.

Descriptive verbs take it too: 편찮으세요 ('is unwell', of an elder), 바쁘세요. And in questions it is how you ask after someone's parents: 아버지는 잘 지내세요? ('Is your father well?').
Give me the honorific vocabulary swaps I need — the verbs and nouns that completely change form for elders.

When the subject is someone you honor, everyday words swap for dedicated honorific forms. The essential set:

| Plain | Honorific | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 먹다 | 드시다 / 잡수시다 | to eat |
| 마시다 | 드시다 | to drink |
| 자다 | 주무시다 | to sleep |
| 있다 | 계시다 | to be/stay |
| 아프다 | 편찮으시다 | to be sick |
| 죽다 | 돌아가시다 | to pass away |
| 말 | 말씀 | speech/words |
| 나이 | 연세 | age |
| 이름 | 성함 | name |
| 집 | 댁 | house |
| 밥 | 진지 | rice/meal |
| 사람 | 분 | person (counter) |
| 생일 | 생신 | birthday |

Usage is all-or-nothing within the phrase: 할아버지께서 진지를 드세요 — subject particle 께서, honorific noun 진지, honorific verb 드시다 carrying -시-. Mixing levels (할아버지가 밥을 드세요) sounds off.

Two cautions. 드시다 covers both eating and drinking, which simplifies life. And these forms describe the honored person's actions, never yours: 'I ate' is always 제가 먹었어요, even to royalty. Your side of the sentence uses humble forms instead — that is the other half of the system.
Honorifics raise the other person. What lowers me? I keep hearing 저 instead of 나.

That is the humble axis (겸양), and 저 is its flagship: 나 (I/me, plain) becomes 저 when speaking politely, and 나가 becomes 제가 — never 저가. 저는 학생이에요, 제가 하겠습니다. In 반말, 나 returns; mixing 저 with 반말 endings sounds broken, so the pairings are 나 + 해체, 저 + 해요체/합니다체.

Beyond pronouns, Korean has humble verbs that lower the speaker's action toward an elevated receiver: 주다 (give) → 드리다: 선생님께 책을 드렸어요 ('I gave the teacher a book'). 묻다 (ask) → 여쭙다/여쭤보다: 여쭤볼 게 있어요 ('there's something I'd like to ask'). 보다 (see/meet) → 뵙다: 내일 뵙겠습니다 ('I'll see you tomorrow', to a superior). 데리다/모시다 handles accompanying an elder: 할머니를 모시고 갔어요.

The logic is relational geometry: raise the other, lower yourself, and the distance between you reads as respect. You never use humble forms about a third party who outranks the person you are lowering toward — in company Korean, your own boss gets lowered when speaking to a client (저희 부장님은... with plain forms), which surprises learners but follows the geometry faithfully: the client is up, everyone on your side is down.
께서 and 께 look almost identical. One is for subjects and one is for 'to', right? How do I keep them straight?

Right, and confusing them is one of the most common mid-level errors. 께서 is the honorific subject particle — it replaces 이/가 when the subject is honored: 할아버지께서 오셨어요 ('Grandfather came'), 선생님께서 말씀하셨어요 ('The teacher spoke'). It answers 'who did it?'.

께 is the honorific 'to' particle — it replaces 에게/한테 when the recipient is honored: 선생님께 드렸어요 ('I gave it to the teacher'), 부모님께 전화했어요 ('I called my parents'). It answers 'to whom?'.

The sentences can combine both: 할아버지께서 저에게... no — watch the full frame: 선생님께서 (subject) 학생들에게 (to students, plain recipients) 책을 주셨어요. And: 제가 (I, humble subject) 선생님께 (to teacher) 여쭤봤어요.

Memory anchor: 께서 contains 서, and you can think of it as 서 있는 사람 — the person standing in the subject position. More practically: if the English role is 'the one who verbs', it is 께서; if it is 'the one receiving', it is 께. Also note 께서 never appears with 계시다 sentences wrongly — 어머니께서 집에 계세요 is exactly right, with 께서 marking the honored subject of the honorific verb.
높임말 동사에는 어떤 것들이 있나요? 자주 쓰는 것만 골라 주세요.

높임 동사는 주어를 높일 때 쓰는 특별한 동사예요. 일상에서 가장 자주 쓰는 것들을 골라 보면 이래요. '먹다'와 '마시다'는 '드시다'가 돼요. '할머니, 진지 드세요'처럼요. '자다'는 '주무시다'가 돼서 '아버지가 주무세요'라고 해요. '있다'는 '계시다'가 돼요. '선생님은 교실에 계세요'처럼요.

몸 상태를 나타내는 말도 바뀌어요. '아프다'는 '편찮으시다'가 돼요. '할아버지께서 편찮으세요'처럼 주어 조사와 '-시-'까지 함께 높여요. '죽다'는 완곡하게 '돌아가시다'라고 해요.

반대로 자신을 낮추는 동사도 있어요. '주다'는 '드리다', '묻다'는 '여쭙다', '보다'는 '뵙다'가 돼요. '선생님께 여쭤봤어요', '내일 뵙겠습니다'처럼 써요.

중요한 점은 높임 동사는 높이는 대상의 행동에만 쓴다는 거예요. 자기가 먹는 것은 아무리 정중한 자리에서도 '제가 먹었어요'예요. 그리고 '말씀'처럼 명사가 바뀌는 경우도 있어요. '말'은 '말씀', '나이'는 '연세', '이름'은 '성함'으로 높여요. 자주 쓰는 열 개 정도만 익혀도 일상 회화의 높임말은 대부분 해결돼요.
안녕, 안녕하세요, 안녕하십니까 — three hellos. Who gets which?

They are the same greeting at three altitudes. 안녕 is 반말: for close friends, younger siblings, children — and only them. Waving 안녕 at a stranger or elder is a real faux pas. 안녕하세요 is 해요체: the universal safe hello for adults — shopkeepers, coworkers, neighbors, anyone you would nod to politely. 안녕하십니까 is 합쇼체: ceremonial and formal — speeches, official events, very formal first meetings, the military.

The word itself means 'are you at peace?' (안녕 = peace/well-being), which is why it doubles as a question about someone's health when stretched: 요즘 안녕하세요? carries a hint of 'have you been well?'.

Timing note: 안녕하세요 works at every hour — Korean has no separate good morning/afternoon/evening for general use (좋은 아침이에요 exists as a calque but 안녕하세요 is what people actually say). One greeting, all day, three politeness settings.

If you remember one: 안녕하세요. It is never wrong with an adult, and upgrading to 안녕하십니까 is only needed when the whole situation is formal, not just the person.
Why are there two goodbyes — 안녕히 가세요 and 안녕히 계세요? Who gets which one?

Because Korean goodbye tracks who is moving. 가세요 (from 가다, 'to go') is said to the person who is leaving: you are staying, they depart — 안녕히 가세요, 'go in peace'. 계세요 (from 계시다, the honorific 'to stay/be') is said to the person who is staying while you leave: 안녕히 계세요, 'stay in peace'.

The classic scene: a guest leaves a friend's home. The guest says 안녕히 계세요 (you're staying here), and the host replies 안녕히 가세요 (you're going). Same doorstep, two different goodbyes, both correct — swapping them produces a moment of confusion, since you'd be telling the host to go in peace from their own house.

In shops, the staff say 안녕히 가세요 to departing customers (and 감사합니다). On the phone neither fits, so common closers are 그럼 들어가세요 — literally 'go in', said to someone at home to mean 'go in and rest' — or simply 또 연락할게요 ('I'll be in touch').

The 반말 pair shrinks to 잘 가 ('go well', to the leaver) and 잘 있어 ('stay well', to the stayer), and the all-purpose casual wave is 안녕 — which is why 안녕 serves as both hello and goodbye among friends.
There seem to be several ways to say thank you and sorry in Korean. Can you rank them?

Both words come in politeness ladders, and climbing one rung too high is always safer than one too low.

Thank you: 고마워 (반말, close friends) → 고마워요 (해요체) → 감사합니다 / 고맙습니다 (formal; 감사합니다 is the most standard and a touch more formal than 고맙습니다, which feels slightly warmer). For something received with real deference: 대단히 감사합니다. Note the response is 별말씀을요 ('don't mention it') or 아니에요 ('not at all').

Sorry: 미안 (반말) → 미안해요 (해요체) → 죄송합니다 (formal — 'I have no face to show', used for real faults and in service settings) → 죄송해요 (mid-formal, very common). 실례합니다 is a different tool: 'excuse me' for interrupting, passing, or entering — a social lubricant, not an apology.

The practical split: 미안해요 is for people, 죄송합니다 is for situations with responsibility — bumping a friend vs being late to a client. Staff in Korea say 죄송합니다 constantly because service culture runs on it. And for a bumped stranger on the subway, a quick 죄송합니다 with a nod is exactly calibrated.
When is 반말 actually okay? I hear it constantly in dramas and I don't want to offend anyone.

반말 (plain speech) is okay in exactly three territories: close friends of similar age where it has been mutually established, family and children, and talking to yourself or animals. In dramas, the 반말 you hear flows between people whose relationships the show has established — spouses, childhood friends, parents to kids. What dramas rarely show is the negotiation that got them there.

In real life, Koreans often make it explicit: 말을 놓자 ('let's drop the speech') is a small social ceremony, usually proposed by the older or senior person. Until that moment, even friendly peers often stay in 해요체 for months. Age matters enormously: a one- or two-year gap can sustain 존댓말 between colleagues for years.

Danger zones: service workers (always 해요체 to them, even though some older customers use 반말 downward — do not imitate that), elders, anyone at work above you, and any stranger.

The foreigner clause is real: Koreans forgive learners' 반말 slips far more readily than natives'. But the asymmetry is your friend — defaulting to 존댓말 never offends, while 반말 presumption can. Learn 반말 receptively first (you need it for dramas, songs, and close friendships later), produce 해요체, and let Koreans invite you down.
조사 '도'와 '만'은 어떻게 써요? 반대말 같아 보이는데요.

네, 두 조사는 반대 방향으로 일해요. '도'는 범위를 넓히는 조사로 '또한'이라는 뜻이에요. '저도 가요'는 나도 다른 사람들처럼 간다는 뜻이고, '커피도 주세요'는 커피까지 추가로 달라는 뜻이에요. '도'는 주어나 목적어 조사를 대신해서 붙어요. '저는'이 '저도'가 되고, '를'이 사라지고 '커피도'가 되는 식이에요. 다만 '에'나 '에서' 뒤에는 그대로 붙을 수 있어요. '서울에도 눈이 와요'처럼요.

'만'은 범위를 좁히는 조사로 '오직'이라는 뜻이에요. '이것만 주세요'는 이것 하나만 달라는 뜻이고, '저만 몰랐어요'는 나만 몰랐다는 뜻이에요. '만'도 주어와 목적어 조사를 대신해요.

두 조사를 함께 쓰는 표현도 있어요. '이것도 저것도 좋아요'는 둘 다 좋다는 뜻이에요. 정리하면, 더하고 싶으면 '도', 하나만 고르고 싶으면 '만'을 쓰면 돼요. 회화에서는 '저도요'라는 대답이 아주 자주 나오니까 먼저 익혀 두면 좋아요.
What Korean do I need for a first business meeting? I don't want to sound like a textbook or a drama.

Business Korean runs on 합쇼체-lite: -입니다 endings for statements about facts, 해요체 warmth in small talk, and a handful of fixed phrases that do heavy lifting. The core set: 처음 뵙겠습니다 ('pleased to meet you', humble 뵙다), 명함을 건네며 저는 마케팅팀의 김민준입니다 ('I'm Kim Minjun from the marketing team' — Koreans introduce team before name), 잘 부탁드립니다 ('I look forward to working with you' — untranslatable and indispensable), 수고하십니다/수고하세요 for greeting working people, 알겠습니다 ('understood', your default reply), and 검토해 보겠습니다 ('we'll review it') for non-committal closes.

Titles do the respect work: call people by 성 + 직함 + 님 — 김 부장님, 이 과장님 — never by bare name, and hand business cards with two hands or supported right hand, receiving theirs the same way and actually reading it.

Sentence endings in reports go up a register: -입니다, -됩니다, -하겠습니다 (future commitment: 내일까지 보내드리겠습니다 'I'll send it by tomorrow', with humble 드리다). Meanwhile, avoid drama-learned phrases and avoid 너/당신 entirely — address people by title or not at all; Korean happily drops pronouns.

Realistic goal for a first meeting: greetings, introductions, 알겠습니다, 감사합니다, and closing 다음에 또 뵙겠습니다. Depth can be 해요체; the frame must be formal.
Why did my Korean coworker ask my age within five minutes of meeting me? It felt rude, but she seemed to need the answer.

She did need it — Korean grammar runs on relative age. Before she can speak to you naturally, she must know whether you are older (형/오빠/누나/언니 territory, 존댓말 obligatory), younger, or 동갑 (same age — the only relationship where 반말 is quickly available between adults). Your age is not trivia in Korea; it is the setting that configures every verb ending she will use with you.

This is why the question 나이가 어떻게 되세요? ('How does your age turn out?' — note the softening) arrives early, often alongside 학번 (university entry year) or 띠 (zodiac year) as gentler proxies. Among Koreans it is as neutral as asking what someone does.

The system has real warmth in it: same-age strangers can become 친구 ('friends' — a word that in Korean literally implies same age) fast, and the 언니/형 relationships carry genuine familial affection.

For you as a foreigner: answer plainly, and feel free to ask back — 어떻게 되세요? is expected reciprocity. If you would rather not say, 요즘 나이는 숫자에 불과하죠 ('age is just a number these days') with a smile deflects gracefully, and Koreans will usually then simply default to 존댓말, which costs nobody anything.
What is Konglish? My Korean friend keeps saying words I almost recognize.

Konglish is English vocabulary that moved to Korea, got Korean pronunciation and sometimes a brand-new meaning, and now lives as ordinary Korean. The safe zone: 핸드폰 (haendeu-pon, 'hand phone' = cell phone), 컴퓨터 (computer), 에어컨 (air conditioner), 노트북 (laptop — a 'notebook'), 셀카 (self-camera = selfie), 아파트 (apartment building), 택시, 버스, 아이스크림. These mean roughly what they sound like, and you can use them freely.

Then there is the fun zone: 화이팅 (from 'fighting') is not about fighting at all — it is the universal cheer, 'you've got this!'. 콘센트 (from 'concentric plug') means an electrical outlet. 사이다 (from 'cider') is a lemon-lime soda like Sprite. 스킨십 (skinship) means physical affection — hand-holding, hugs — not dermatology.

Konglish is not 'bad English'; it is Korean vocabulary with English ancestry, like English 'rendezvous' is French ancestry. Koreans do not expect it to work in London or Los Angeles, and part of fluency is knowing which words are local. Enjoy the almost-recognition, but flag the fun-zone words: they are exactly the ones that will betray you abroad and delight you in Seoul.
Which Konglish words will actually trick me — the ones whose meaning changed completely?

The traps are words whose English original points you the wrong way:

미팅 (miting): not a business meeting (that is 회의) — a group blind date among university students. Being invited to a 미팅 is a social event, not a calendar item.

원룸 (one-room): a studio apartment. 오피스텔 (officetel): a studio in a mixed office-residential building. Neither translates word-for-word into English real-estate terms.

와이셔츠 (wai-syeocheu, 'white shirt' compressed): any men's dress shirt, whatever its color.

사인 (sain): an autograph when fans ask, but a signature on documents is 서명 — asking a celebrity for a 사인 is right; 'signing' a contract with 사인 is Konglish bleed.

핸들 (handle): the steering wheel of a car, not any handle (that is 손잡이).

서비스 (service): in restaurants, something free on the house — 서비스예요 from staff means 'this one's free', a beloved word.

개그맨 (gag man): a TV comedian. 나이트 (night): a nightclub for an older crowd.

The pattern to notice: Konglish usually narrows a broad English word to one specific Korean use. Learn each as its own vocabulary item with its Korean meaning, and never trust the English echo.
콩글리시란 무엇인가요? 예를 들어서 설명해 주세요.

콩글리시는 영어 단어가 한국에 들어와서 한국어처럼 쓰이는 말이에요. 발음이 한국식으로 바뀌고, 가끔은 뜻까지 달라져요. 예를 들어 '핸드폰'은 휴대폰을 뜻하고, '에어컨', '노트북', '셀카' 같은 말은 한국 사람이라면 누구나 매일 써요. 이런 말은 영어 단어를 빌려왔지만, 이제는 한국어의 일부예요.

뜻이 달라진 콩글리시는 특히 재미있어요. '화이팅'은 싸우라는 뜻이 아니라 '힘내라'는 응원이에요. '콘센트'는 전기를 꽂는 곳을 뜻하고, '사이다'는 탄산음료를 뜻해요. '미팅'은 회사 회의가 아니라 대학생들의 단체 소개팅을 말하는 경우가 많아요. 진짜 회의는 '회의'라고 해요.

콩글리시는 틀린 영어가 아니에요. 한국에서 생활하려면 꼭 알아야 하는 생활 단어예요. 다만 영어권 나라에서는 통하지 않는 말이 많으니까, 외국에서 쓸 때는 조심해야 해요. 한국 친구와 이야기할 때는 콩글리시를 알면 대화가 훨씬 자연스러워져요.
How do Koreans introduce themselves? I want the full first-meeting script.

The frame is fixed and mercifully short. Bow slightly, then: 안녕하세요, 처음 뵙겠습니다 ('Hello, this is my first time meeting you' — 뵙겠습니다 is the humble form). Then your name with 저는: 저는 사라입니다. Add affiliation before or after as context demands: 미국에서 왔어요 ('I came from America'), 한국어를 공부하고 있어요 ('I'm studying Korean'). Close with 만나서 반갑습니다 ('glad to meet you') or 잘 부탁드립니다 ('I ask for your good care' — the social all-purpose closer).

If they ask your name formally, the question itself is a lesson: 성함이 어떻게 되세요? — 성함 is the honorific word for 'name' and 되세요 softens it. Answer plainly: 제 이름은 사라예요. (Your own name takes no honorifics — humility axis again.)

What not to do: do not extend a hand automatically in formal settings (bows lead; handshakes often come with a bow and the left hand supporting the right arm), do not use the other person's first name alone, and do not say 당신 for 'you' — Korean introductions work beautifully with zero 'you' at all.

Full model: 안녕하세요, 처음 뵙겠습니다. 저는 미국에서 온 사라입니다. 한국어를 공부하고 있어요. 만나서 반갑습니다. — Fifteen seconds, every piece doing social work.
Phone calls in Korean start with 여보세요. What else is different about Korean phone etiquette?

여보세요 is the dedicated phone hello — it is used only for answering calls, never face to face. The caller identifies themselves first: 안녕하세요, 저는 김민준입니다 or 회사 이름 + 입니다. If you need someone else: 혹시 박 선생님 계세요? ('Is Mr. Park there?' — with honorific 계세요). To ask who is calling: 누구세요? or 실례지만 누구시죠?.

Key phrases: 바꿔 주세요 ('please put them on'), 잠시만 기다려 주세요 ('please wait a moment'), 전화 잘못 거셨어요 ('you have the wrong number'), 끊을게요 ('I'll hang up now' — said before ending, since abrupt hang-ups are rude), 나중에 다시 걸게요 ('I'll call again later'), 통화 중이에요 ('the line is busy').

Notice what is absent: you never open with your own number or 'hello?' uncertainty the way English does, and 여보세요 carries a built-in 'I'm listening' warmth.

Texting has its own register: 카톡 (KakaoTalk) messages to elders still run 존댓말, and the little ㅎㅎ/ㅋㅋ laughter strings calibrate softness. A bare 네 (yes) can read cold in text; 네~ or 넵 adds warmth — 넵 is the perky, slightly military-crisp 'yes!' beloved of young workers answering bosses.
Can I mix levels a little — like use 저 with casual endings, or 나 with formal ones? Native speakers seem to bend rules.

Native speakers bend them along predictable lines; learners mostly break them by accident, and the two sound different. The hard constraints: 저 (humble I) pairs only with 존댓말 endings, and 나 pairs only with 반말 or 해요체-with-caution. 제가 갑니다 is right; 제가 가 (with 반말 ending) is a classic learner error that sounds like two sentences colliding. 나는 갑니다 is stiff-wrong in the other direction: formal ending, plain pronoun — it reads as a child playing soldier or a historical drama.

Where natives genuinely mix: (1) 해요체 with -시- honorifics about a third person — 엄마가 오셨어요 mid-polite-conversation is normal layering, not mixing errors. (2) 반말 with softening 요 sprinkled in (준말/반존대) among close-but-not-equal friends — 가지 마요 to a slightly older close friend. (3) 혼잣말 (self-talk) in 반말 even to elders' faces is impossible — but thinking aloud in plain form while working is universal.

The safe learner rule: pick one level per conversation and hold it; let the pronoun, the particle set (이/가 vs 께서), and the endings all agree. Native mixing is jazz — you have to know the tune cold before you improvise on it.
What do 잘 먹겠습니다 and 잘 먹었습니다 mean exactly? Koreans say them at every meal.

They are the bookends of a Korean meal, and both are humble gratitude formulas. Before eating: 잘 먹겠습니다 — literally 'I will eat well', functioning as 'thank you for this food' to whoever provided it: the host, the cook, the person paying. After eating: 잘 먹었습니다 — 'I ate well', thanking them again.

Say them to the person who treated you, to the host at a home, even to restaurant staff when someone else is paying. If you cooked and others thank you, the reply is 많이 드세요 ('eat a lot', with honorific 드세요).

Related table phrases: 먼저 드세요 ('please start first', to elders — you wait for them), 맛있게 드세요 ('enjoy your meal', said by staff and hosts), 더 드세요 ('have more'). And when an elder is served, 받으세요... the serving etiquette pairs with two hands for pouring drinks for seniors, turning your head aside when drinking in front of them — traditional, still observed in formal settings.

Do you say 잘 먹겠습니다 alone or for fast food? Koreans do say it to themselves quietly (혼잣말) or among friends with a grin — the formula is that ingrained. Skipping it at a Korean home dinner would be noticed; using it never is.
'께'와 '에게'는 어떻게 달라요? 둘 다 영어로는 'to'라고 배웠어요.

두 조사 모두 받는 사람을 나타내지만, 높임의 정도가 달라요. '에게'는 일반적인 조사로, 글이나 공식적인 말에서 자주 써요. '학생에게 공지했어요', '친구에게 편지를 보냈어요'처럼요. 말로 할 때는 '에게'보다 '한테'가 더 자연스러워요. '친구한테 말했어요'처럼요.

'께'는 높이는 대상에게 쓰는 조사예요. 선생님이나 부모님, 할아버지처럼 존경하는 분이 받는 사람일 때 써요. '선생님께 책을 드렸어요', '부모님께 전화했어요'처럼요. '께'는 보통 '드리다', '여쭙다' 같은 낮춤 동사와 함께 쓰여서 문장 전체의 높임이 맞아요.

그래서 '친구께'라고 하면 어색하고, '선생님에게'라고 하면 예의가 부족하게 들릴 수 있어요. 받는 사람이 누구인지에 따라 고르면 돼요.

비슷한 이름의 '께서'와는 완전히 다른 조사예요. '께서'는 주어를 높이는 조사라서 '할아버지께서 오셨어요'처럼 행동하는 사람을 높이고, '께'는 받는 사람을 나타내요. 두 조사가 한 문장에 같이 올 수도 있어요. '할아버지께서 선생님께 인사하셨어요'처럼요.
Why do Koreans never seem to say 'you'? I was told 당신 is dangerous. What do I use instead?

Because Korean social grammar makes 'you' the hardest word in the language. 당신, the dictionary 'you', is confrontational in most real contexts — spouses use it affectionately, strangers use it when a fight is starting ('당신이 뭔데요?' — 'who do you think you are?'). 너 is 반말-only, for children and intimate friends. 그쪽 ('that side') works for strangers in some service contexts but can sound distant.

What Koreans actually do: omit 'you' (context carries it), or use the person's title or role: 선생님 ('teacher' — used for doctors, elders, any respected person), 사장님 ('boss/owner' — to shop owners), 기사님 (to drivers), 이모/언니 in restaurants to female staff in casual settings, 손님 ('guest/customer'). Or use name + 씨 in workplaces: 민준 씨. Or kinship-style terms: 아주머니, 아저씨 for middle-aged strangers.

This is not evasion — Korean is a language where relationships, not pronouns, address people. The sentence '___는 어디에 사세요?' with a title in the blank is warmer and more correct than any pronoun could be.

Learner rule: when you want to say 'you', first try deleting it; if the sentence wobbles, insert a title. You will sound more Korean with a missing pronoun than with a perfect 당신.
Fix these honorific mistakes for me: '할아버지가 밥을 먹어요', '선생님이 저를 주셨어요' (I mean the teacher gave it to me), '제가 선생님한테 말씀했어요'.

Three sentences, three different honorific axes breaking.

1. 할아버지가 밥을 먹어요 → 할아버지께서 진지를 드세요 (or 잡수세요). Everything rises together: subject particle 께서, meal noun 진지, verb 드시다 with -시-. Your version used plain forms for a grandfather — grammatically fine, socially flat.

2. 선생님이 저를 주셨어요 is wrong in an interesting way: 주시다 is the honorific of 주다 used when the giver is honored — 선생님께서 저에게 주셨어요 is actually correct for 'the teacher gave it to me', because the honored subject is the giver. Your original failed only on case: the recipient 'me' needs 에게, not 를 — 주다 takes a recipient (에게) plus a thing (을): 선생님께서 저에게 책을 주셨어요. The real trap is the reverse: 'I gave it to the teacher' must be 제가 선생님께 책을 드렸어요, with humble 드리다, because now the giver is you.

3. 제가 선생님한테 말씀했어요 → 제가 선생님께 말씀드렸어요. Two fixes: recipient of speech to a superior takes 께, and 'to say (to an elder)' is 말씀드리다 — 말씀 is the honorific noun for speech, and your speaking to them is a humble act of 'offering words'. Note the mirror trap: 선생님의 말씀 ('the teacher's words') uses 말씀 as pure honorific noun, while your words upward are 말씀드리는 것. Direction decides everything in this system.
Korean has two number systems. Give me the map of which one goes where, because I keep using the wrong one.

The split is by job, not by size. Native Korean numbers (하나, 둘, 셋, 넷, 다섯, 여섯, 일곱, 여덟, 아홉, 열, 스물, 서른, 마흔, 쉰) handle counting things with counters, age, and clock hours: 사과 세 개 ('three apples'), 스물다섯 살 ('25 years old'), 세 시 ('3 o'clock'). Sino-Korean numbers (일, 이, 삼, 사, 오, 육, 칠, 팔, 구, 십, 백, 천, 만) handle dates, money, minutes, seconds, floors, and phone numbers: 삼월 오일 ('March 5'), 오천 원 ('5,000 won'), 십 분 ('10 minutes'), 삼 층 ('3rd floor').

The clock is the famous split-brain case: hours native, minutes Sino — 세 시 십오 분 is 3:15. Ages are native (살), but formal documents may use 세... in practice everyone says native for age.

Native numbers only run comfortably to 99 and are rarely used past 39 in speech; anything big — prices, populations, years — is Sino territory: 2026년 is 이천이십육 년.

Memory rule: if you are counting objects you could hold, or telling your age or the hour, go native. If it is measured, dated, priced, or numbered, go Sino.
Korean counters are new to me. Which ones do I actually need for daily life?

Korean counts noun + number + counter, and the counter matches the kind of thing. The daily dozen:

| Counter | Counts | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 개 | general things | 사과 세 개 (3 apples) |
| 명 | people | 학생 두 명 (2 students) |
| 분 | people, honorific | 손님 세 분 (3 guests) |
| 마리 | animals | 개 한 마리 (1 dog) |
| 권 | books | 책 두 권 (2 books) |
| 잔 | cupfuls | 커피 한 잔 (1 coffee) |
| 병 | bottles | 맥주 두 병 (2 beers) |
| 대 | machines, cars | 자동차 한 대 (1 car) |
| 장 | flat things | 종이 세 장 (3 sheets) |
| 벌 | clothing sets/outfits | 옷 한 벌 (1 outfit) |
| 켤레 | paired footwear | 양말 한 켤레 (1 pair of socks) |
| 송이 | flowers, bunches | 꽃 한 송이 (1 flower) |
| 자루 | long handled things | 연필 한 자루 (1 pencil) |

Numbers before counters are native, and the first four change shape: 하나→한 개, 둘→두 개, 셋→세 개, 넷→네 개, 스물→스무 개. Word order is noun first, then number + counter: 사과 세 개, never 세 개 사과 in neutral speech.

When in doubt, 개 is the forgiving default — Koreans will understand 사과 세 개 and even 사람 세 개 (understood, though 명 is correct). Counters are polish, not a barrier.
한국어에서는 왜 주어를 자주 생략해요? 영어에서는 주어가 꼭 있어야 하잖아요.

한국어는 문맥 중심의 언어이기 때문이에요. 대화에서는 누가 말하고 있는지, 무엇을 말하는지 상황이 알려 주는 경우가 많아서, 주어를 굳이 말하지 않아도 뜻이 통해요. 예를 들어 친구와 밥을 먹으면서 '먹었어?'라고만 해도 '너는 밥을 먹었어?'라는 뜻이 분명해요. 오히려 주어를 매번 넣으면 부자연스럽고, 때로는 딱딱하거나 강조하는 느낌까지 줘요.

주제를 한 번 정해 놓는 것도 이유예요. '저는 학생이에요. 한국어를 공부해요'처럼 처음에 '저는'으로 주제를 정하면, 다음 문장에서는 주어 없이도 계속 그 사람 이야기인 줄 알아요.

또 한국어는 동사 끝에서 듣는 사람과의 관계가 드러나기 때문에, 주어가 없어도 문장이 완성돼요. 물론 주어가 꼭 필요한 경우도 있어요. 여러 사람이 등장해서 누가 한 행동인지 헷갈릴 때나, 강조하고 싶을 때는 주어를 분명히 말해요. '제가 할게요'처럼요.

영어가 문법으로 주어를 요구하는 언어라면, 한국어는 상황에서 주어를 읽는 언어예요. 그래서 한국어를 잘하려면 단어만이 아니라 앞뒤 맥락을 읽는 연습이 중요해요.
Why does 하나 become 한 in 한 개, and 둘 become 두? The numbers change shape before counters.

Four native numbers put on a shorter form before counters: 하나 → 한, 둘 → 두, 셋 → 세, 넷 → 네, and 스물 → 스무. So you get 한 개, 두 명, 세 시, 네 마리, 스무 살. The full forms 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷 are for counting aloud in the abstract (하나, 둘, 셋! when counting off) or standing alone; the short forms are attributive — they exist to lean on a counter.

Why? These are ancient adjective-like forms of the numbers; Korean numbers historically behaved like modifiers, and the language kept the clipped shapes in the modifier slot. English has a faint echo: 'one' vs the 'a/an' that descends from it.

The same shortening shows up beyond counters: 한 번 ('once'), 두 번, 세 번째 ('third'), 한 사람 ('one person').

Practical handling: memorize the five pairs as units — 한/두/세/네/스무 + counter — because 1, 2, 3, 4, and 20 are the numbers you will say most. From 다섯 upward, nothing changes: 다섯 개, 여섯 명, 일곱 시, all plain. It is a small, closed irregularity at the exact spot where beginners live, which is annoying but also means you will drill it constantly just by surviving.
How do big numbers work in Korean money? 만 seems to do a lot of heavy lifting.

Korean groups large numbers by 만 (10,000), not by thousands, and that single fact reorganizes all money talk. 만 원 is 10,000 won. 십만 원 is 100,000. 백만 원 is 1,000,000. 천만 원 is 10,000,000. Then the next unit is 억 (100,000,000): 일억 원 is 100 million won.

So a price of 250,000 won is 이십오만 원 ('two-ten-five ten-thousands'), and a 1.2-billion-won apartment is 십이억 원. English speakers must stop converting digit-by-digit and start hearing 만 as the comma: Korean commas in prices mentally sit every four digits.

All of this is Sino-Korean: 만, 억, and the digits 일 이 삼 사 오 육 칠 팔 구 십 백 천. The month names carry two fossils of their own: June is 유월 and October is 시월, not 육월/십월 — the only two months that break the pattern, smoothed for ease of pronunciation centuries ago.

Phone numbers are also read in Sino digits, with 0 as 공 or 영: 010 is 공일공. And years: 2026년 is 이천이십육 년, read as a full number, not 'twenty twenty-six'.
How are dates and days of the week said in Korean? I need to survive a calendar conversation.

Dates run big-to-small: year, month, day. 2026년 11월 27일 — 년 (year), 월 (month), 일 (day), all Sino-Korean numbers. Months are just number + 월: 일월, 이월, 삼월, 사월, 오월, then the two fossils 유월 (June, not 육월) and 시월 (October, not 십월), 십일월, 십이월.

Days of the week are one syllable + 요일, each named for a classical element:

| Day | Korean | Element |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | 월요일 | moon |
| Tuesday | 화요일 | fire |
| Wednesday | 수요일 | water |
| Thursday | 목요일 | wood |
| Friday | 금요일 | metal/gold |
| Saturday | 토요일 | earth |
| Sunday | 일요일 | sun |

Relative days: 오늘 (today), 내일 (tomorrow), 모레 (day after tomorrow), 어제 (yesterday), 그제 (day before yesterday), 이번 주 (this week), 다음 주 (next week), 지난주 (last week).

Asking the date: 오늘이 며칠이에요? ('What date is it today?') — 며칠 means 'what day (of the month)'. Asking the weekday: 무슨 요일이에요? ('What day of the week is it?'). Answer: 11월 27일 금요일이에요. Calendar Korean is mercifully regular — learn the two fossil months and the seven 요일 and you own it.
What do -지요 and -죠 actually add? Sentences seem complete without them.

-지요 (contracted to -죠) adds 'as you (should) know' — it seeks agreement or states something presented as shared knowledge. 날씨가 좋죠? ('The weather's nice, isn't it?'), 내일 회의가 있죠?
