('There's a meeting tomorrow, right?'), 그럼요, 당연하죠 ('of course, obviously'). The speaker is not neutrally informing; they are confirming common ground.

It also softens commands into friendly instructions: 이쪽으로 오시죠 ('come this way, if you would'), 천천히 하죠. In announcements and gentle guidance, -죠 keeps authority from sounding blunt.

Compare the plain ending: 내일 회의가 있어요 is a flat announcement. 내일 회의가 있죠? checks that the listener also knows. 내일 회의가 있어요? asks for information you lack. Three different social acts, three endings.

With past tense it becomes -았/었죠: 그때는 어렸죠 ('I was young back then' — said with shared nostalgia), and in 반말 it is -지: 알지? ('you know, right?'), 그렇지 ('that's right').

Learners underuse -죠 for years, then discover it is the sound of Korean rapport. Whenever your English brain adds 'right?', 'isn't it?', or 'as you know', -죠 is probably the ending Korean wants.
'안'과 '못'의 부정 차이를 설명해 주세요. 둘 다 'not' 아닌가요?

둘 다 부정이지만, 뜻이 분명히 달라요. '안'은 의지나 단순한 부정을 나타내요. '안 가요'는 가고 싶지 않거나 그냥 가지 않는다는 뜻이고, '안 먹어요'는 먹지 않는다는 뜻이에요. 말하는 사람의 선택이나 사실의 부재를 말할 때 써요.

'못'은 능력이 안 되거나 사정이 있어서 할 수 없다는 뜻이에요. '못 가요'는 가고 싶어도 사정이 있어서 못 간다는 뜻이고, '수영을 못 해요'는 수영할 줄 모른다는 뜻이에요. 그래서 약속에 못 갈 때는 '안 가요'가 아니라 '못 가요'라고 해야 실례가 안 돼요. '안 가요'는 가기 싫다는 뜻으로 들릴 수 있거든요.

긴 부정문도 있어요. '가지 않아요'는 '안 가요'와 뜻이 같지만 조금 더 정중하고 글에서 자주 써요. '가지 못해요'는 '못 가요'와 같은 뜻이에요.

정리하면, 마음의 문제면 '안', 능력과 사정의 문제면 '못'이에요. 이 구분 하나만으로도 한국 사람과의 대화에서 오해가 많이 줄어요.
What are -잖아요 and -거든요 for? My Korean friends end sentences with them constantly.

Both endings manage shared knowledge, in opposite directions. -잖아요 means 'you know / as I (may have) mentioned / isn't it obvious' — it reminds the listener of something they know or should know: 어제 말했잖아요 ('I told you yesterday!'), 여기 맛있잖아요 ('this place is delicious, you know it is'), 비 오잖아요 ('it's raining, as you can see'). It can warm a conversation or deliver an affectionate scolding; tone decides.

-거든요 explains or supplies a reason the listener did not have: 사실 제가 먼저 도착했거든요 ('actually, I arrived first' — new background info), 요즘 바쁘거든요 ('the thing is, I'm busy these days'). It answers an unspoken 'why?' and is the classic way to start giving context: 저 사실은 한국 사람이 아니거든요 ('actually, I'm not Korean, you see').

So -잖아요 points backward at shared ground ('you already know this'), and -거든요 lays new ground ('here's what you didn't know'). English approximations: -잖아요 ≈ 'you know', 'after all'; -거든요 ≈ 'the thing is', 'you see'.

Both are everywhere in speech and rare in writing. Mastering them will not change your grammar scores much, but it will change how Korean you sound overnight.
갈까요 and 갈래요 both seem to involve other people. Which is 'shall we' and which is 'I want to'?

갈까요 is the proposal: 'shall we go?' — -(으)ㄹ까요 asks the listener to decide or join. 같이 영화 볼까요? ('shall we watch a movie together?'), 뭘 먹을까요? ('what shall we eat?'), 제가 할까요? ('shall I do it?' — offering). It can also wonder aloud: 비가 올까요? ('do you think it'll rain?').

갈래요 is the declaration of your own will: -(으)ㄹ래요 states what you want to do. 저는 집에 갈래요 ('I'm going home' — my choice), 뭐 먹을래요? asks the listener's preference ('what do you want to eat?'), 커피 마실래요? offers by asking their will ('would you like coffee?').

The contrast sharpens in a café: 뭐 마실까요? = let's decide together; 뭐 마실래요? = tell me your pick. And 저는 커피 마실래요 announces yours.

Watch the negative-space trap: -ㄹ래요 about a third person or in formal settings is off-limits — it voices the subject's own will, so it belongs to the speaker or the addressed listener only. For reporting someone else's wishes, -고 싶어해요 returns.

One more member of the family: -(으)ㄹ게요 promises the listener — 제가 할게요 ('I'll do it'), 내일 전화할게요 ('I'll call tomorrow'). 까요 proposes, 래요 declares, 게요 promises: Korean splits English 'will' into three social acts.
How does -면 work, and is it the same as English 'if'? I also keep seeing -거든 and -(으)ㄹ 때 in similar spots.

-면 is the general conditional: 비가 오면 집에 있을게요 ('if it rains, I'll stay home'), 시간이 있으면 같이 가요 ('if you have time, let's go together'), 한국에 가면 김치를 먹을 거예요. It handles hypotheticals, habits, and whenever-conditions alike — 돈이 많으면 행복할까요? ('if you had lots of money, would you be happy?').

-(으)ㄹ 때 is not 'if' but 'when' — it assumes the moment arrives: 한국에 갈 때 ('when I go to Korea'), 어렸을 때 ('when I was young'). Use 때 for time-points, 면 for conditions that may not happen: 비가 올 때 우산을 써요 (when it rains — a routine) vs 비가 오면 우산을 쓸게요 (if it rains — a plan).

-거든 is the stiff, written conditional ('if indeed'): 필요하거든 말씀하세요 ('if you should need anything, say so') — mostly seen in notices and older speech; recognize it, rarely use it.

Past conditional wishes take -았/었으면 좋겠다: 돈이 있었으면 좋겠어요 ('I wish I had money'), 어제 갔으면 좋았을 텐데요 ('it would have been good if you'd gone yesterday' — counterfactual regret).

One structural note: the -면 clause never carries future tense itself — 비가 오면, not 올면... the standard form is 오면 even for future rain, and the main clause carries the future. English tempts you to mark both clauses; Korean marks only one.
How do I say 'have to', 'may', and 'must not' in Korean? Obligation phrases, please.

Three frames cover the whole territory, all built on -아/어야 and its relatives. Obligation 'have to/must': -아/어야 해요 (or 돼요) — 일찍 일어나야 해요 ('I have to get up early'), 숙제를 해야 해요 ('must do homework'), 가야 돼요. The form literally says 'only if I do X does it work', which is why 해요/돼요 both fit.

Permission 'may': -아/어도 돼요 — 먹어도 돼요 ('you may eat it'), 여기 앉아도 돼요? ('may I sit here?'), 사진을 찍어도 돼요. Answering with 네, 돼요 grants it; the question form is your daily tool in museums, offices, and other people's homes.

Prohibition 'must not': -(으)면 안 돼요 — 여기서 담배를 피우면 안 돼요 ('you must not smoke here'), 늦으면 안 돼요 ('don't be late' — being late won't do), 만지면 안 돼요 ('do not touch').

Softeners matter: -아/어야 해요 can be lightened with -아/어야겠어요 ('I'll have to...'), and obligations about yourself in promises often ride -ㄹ게요. And note the elegant symmetry: -아/어도 돼요 (even if you do it, it's fine) vs -(으)면 안 돼요 (if you do it, it's not fine) — permission and prohibition are mirror images around 돼요.
'께서'는 언제 쓰나요? '이/가'랑 뭐가 달라요?

'께서'는 주어를 높일 때 쓰는 조사예요. 보통 '이/가'와 같은 자리에서 쓰지만, 주어인 사람을 존경한다는 뜻이 더해져요. '할아버지께서 오셨어요', '선생님께서 말씀하셨어요'처럼요. 그래서 '께서'가 오면 동사에도 '-시-'가 함께 붙는 경우가 많아요. '아버지께서 책을 읽으세요'처럼 조사와 동사가 같이 주어를 높이는 거예요.

'께서'를 쓸 수 있는 대상은 사람뿐이에요. 존경의 대상이 아닌 사물이나 동물에는 쓰지 않아요. '비가 와요', '날씨가 좋아요'처럼 일반적인 주어에는 '이/가'를 써요.

비슷한 조사 '께'와 혼동하면 안 돼요. '께'는 받는 사람을 나타내는 조사라서 '선생님께 드렸어요'처럼 쓰고, '께서'는 행동하는 주어를 높여요. 한 문장에 둘 다 들어갈 수도 있어요. '할아버지께서 선생님께 전화하셨어요'처럼요.

또 '께서'는 '계시다'와 함께 쓰는 경우가 아주 많아요. '어머니께서 집에 계세요'가 대표적이에요. 높임말은 조사만 따로 외우는 것보다, 조사와 동사를 한 덩어리로 익히는 것이 훨씬 자연스러워요.
이것, 그것, 저것 — and 여기, 거기, 저기. Is it just near/far like English this/that?

Korean runs a three-way system where English has two, and the middle term is listener-centered. 이- is near the speaker: 이것 ('this thing by me'), 여기 ('here'), 이 사람 ('this person'). 그- is near the listener, or something just mentioned: 그것 ('that thing by you / the one we just talked about'), 거기 ('there by you'), 그 사람 ('that person — the one in our conversation'). 저- is far from both: 저것 ('that thing over there'), 저기 ('over there'), 저 사람 ('that person over there').

The 그- series does double duty as the anaphoric set: 그 책 can mean the book near you or the book we have been discussing, which is why 그 is the most frequent of the three in conversation.

Useful phrases lock these in: 이쪽 ('this way'), 저쪽으로 가세요 ('go that way'), and the attention-getters — 여기요! is the standard call for staff in a restaurant, while 저기요! calls out to someone at a distance and doubles as a general 'excuse me'. And 이거 얼마예요? ('how much is this?') is the shopper's first sentence.

Mnemonic: 이 = me, 그 = you/mentioned, 저 = yonder. English 'that' splits into 그 and 저 depending on whether the listener or shared context anchors it.
무슨, 어떤, 어느, 몇 — all of them seem to mean 'what/which'. Sort them out.

Four question words, four jobs. 무슨 + noun asks 'what kind of / what' in open terms: 무슨 일이에요? ('what's the matter?'), 무슨 요일이에요? ('what day of the week?'), 무슨 뜻이에요? ('what does it mean?'). It wants a content answer.

어떤 + noun asks 'what kind of' with a descriptive or selection flavor: 어떤 음악을 좋아해요? ('what kind of music do you like?'), 어떤 사람이에요? ('what is he like?'). It invites characterization.

어느 + noun asks 'which one' from a set: 어느 나라에서 왔어요? ('which country are you from?'), 어느 쪽이에요? ('which way?'). It presumes options.

몇 asks 'how many / what number': 몇 시예요? ('what time is it?'), 몇 개 주세요? ('how many shall I give you?'), 몇 살이에요? ('how old?'). It always expects a number, and it pairs with counters.

Overlap exists — 무슨 영화 vs 어떤 영화 both get asked — but the centers hold: 무슨 = what (identity), 어떤 = what kind (quality), 어느 = which (choice), 몇 = how many (quantity). English squeezes all four into 'what/which/how many', so expect your brain to reach for one word; Korean asks you to decide what kind of question you are asking.
How do comparisons work? 'Bigger than', 'the biggest' — and is there anything like 'more and more'?

The comparison frame is A는 B보다 + descriptive verb: 오늘은 어제보다 따뜻해요 ('today is warmer than yesterday'), 이게 그것보다 비싸요 ('this is more expensive than that'), 한국어가 영어보다 어려워요? — fighting words, but grammatical. 보다 is the 'than' particle, and 더 ('more') can join for emphasis: 더 커요, 더 빨리.

Superlatives use 제일 or 가장 before the adjective: 제일 좋아요 ('like it most'), 가장 큰 산 ('the biggest mountain'), 제일 먼저 ('first of all'). No form change on the adjective itself — Korean adjectives never inflect for comparison, which learners find merciful.

Progressives exist too: 점점 ('more and more, gradually') — 점점 추워져요 ('it's getting colder and colder'), 날이 갈수록, and the doubled pattern -아/어질수록... simpler: -면 -을수록 means 'the more... the more': 읽으면 읽을수록 재미있어요 ('the more I read, the more interesting it gets'), 바쁠수록 건강을 챙겨야 해요.

And equality: 만큼 — 형만큼 커요 ('as big as my older brother'), 예상만큼 비싸요 ('as expensive as expected'), and 처럼 for 'like/as': 새처럼 날고 싶어요 ('I want to fly like a bird'). The full toolkit: 보다 (than), 제일/가장 (most), 만큼 (as much as), 처럼 (like), 점점 (more and more). Korean comparisons are pure assembly — no -er, -est, or irregular 'better/worse' to memorize.
Why does Korean have four words for older sibling? 형, 오빠, 누나, 언니 — how do I pick?

Because the word encodes two facts at once: the sibling's gender and your gender. A man calls his older brother 형 and his older sister 누나. A woman calls her older brother 오빠 and her older sister 언니. Younger siblings are simpler: 남동생 (younger brother), 여동생 (younger sister), collectively 동생.

Crucially, these terms escape the family. Koreans address slightly older friends, colleagues, and even partners with 형/오빠/누나/언니 — it is the standard warm address for 'older and close'. A woman calling a male friend 오빠 is normal; the word also famously appears in dating contexts, which is context, not definition.

The wider family set: 아버지/아빠 (father, formal/casual), 어머니/엄마 (mother), 할아버지 (grandfather), 할머니 (grandmother), 삼촌 (uncle — father's brother, generic uncle), 이모 (mother's sister), 고모 (father's sister), 외삼촌 (mother's brother) — Korean tracks which side of the family an aunt or uncle belongs to.

For learners: your own siblings get the term from your perspective; when asking about someone else's family, add honor: 형님, 아버님, 어머님. And note the social magic: calling someone 언니 or 형 is itself an act of closeness — Koreans will sometimes invite it explicitly: 언니라고 불러도 돼요 ('you can call me eonni').
한국어의 문장 순서는 영어와 어떻게 달라요?

가장 큰 차이는 동사의 위치예요. 영어는 '주어 + 동사 + 목적어' 순서지만, 한국어는 '주어 + 목적어 + 동사' 순서라서 동사가 항상 마지막에 와요. 'I eat an apple'은 한국어로 '저는 사과를 먹어요'가 돼요. 동사가 마지막에 있기 때문에, 한국어를 들을 때는 문장의 끝까지 들어야 전체 뜻을 알 수 있어요.

수식하는 말의 위치도 달라요. 영어에서는 명사 뒤에 설명이 붙지만, 한국어에서는 명사 앞에 설명이 와요. '내가 어제 산 책'처럼 '책'이라는 명사 앞에 긴 설명이 먼저 와요.

또 한국어는 조사가 발달해서 어순이 비교적 자유로워요. '저는 사과를 먹어요'와 '사과를 저는 먹어요'는 강조점이 조금 다르지만 둘 다 맞는 문장이에요. 조사가 각 단어의 역할을 표시해 주기 때문이에요. 다만 동사는 마지막 자리를 지키는 것이 원칙이에요.

시간과 장소를 나타내는 말은 보통 문장의 앞부분에 와요. '저는 어제 도서관에서 책을 읽었어요'처럼 큰 것에서 작은 것으로, 배경에서 핵심으로 나아가는 흐름이에요. 이 순서에 익숙해지면 한국어 문장이 훨씬 자연스럽게 느껴져요.
가다 and 오다 both confuse me — when is coming 'going' in Korean? My host said 집에 가세요 when I arrived at my own home.

Korean direction verbs are anchored to a reference point, and the anchor can shift to the listener or the home base in ways English does not. 가다 is motion away from the anchor; 오다 is motion toward it. 학교에 가요 (going to school, away), 집에 와요 (coming home — home is the anchor, so arrival home is 'coming' even if you say it while leaving the office: 저 집에 왔어요 texted after arrival, and 집에 갈게요 said while departing are both natural — the anchor flips with your viewpoint in the moment).

Your host's 집에 가세요 was the standard farewell 'go home safely' — from the host's position you are going away. If your mother calls and asks where you are, 지금 집에 가고 있어요 ('I'm on my way home') and 집에 오고 있어요 both occur; 가고 있어요 views the road, 오고 있어요 views home.

Compounds extend the logic: 들어가다 (go in), 들어오다 (come in), 나가다 (go out), 나오다 (come out), 올라가다 (go up), 올라오다 (come up), 내려가다/내려오다 (down), 돌아가다 (go back), 돌아오다 (come back). Waiters say 이쪽으로 오세요 ('come this way') because the anchor is the speaker.

Rule of thumb: if the destination is where the speaker (or the person you're empathizing with) is or belongs, 오다; otherwise 가다. And 갔다 오다 pairs in greetings: 다녀오겠습니다 ('I'll go and come back') when leaving home, 다녀오세요 in reply.
크다 vs 많다, 작다 vs 적다 — both pairs translate as big/many and small/few. What's the actual distinction?

The split is size versus quantity. 크다/작다 measure physical (or abstract) magnitude of one thing: 큰 집 ('a big house'), 작은 가방 ('a small bag'), 목소리가 커요 ('your voice is loud' — volume as size). 많다/적다 measure amount of stuff or people: 사람이 많아요 ('there are many people'), 시간이 적어요 ('there is little time'), 물이 많아요.

So a crowd is not 큰 사람 (that is a physically large person) but 많은 사람. Rain is 비가 많이 와요 ('a lot of rain falls') — 많이, the adverb form of 많다. A big problem can be 큰 문제 (magnitude) — abstract size borrows 크다 legitimately.

The trap pair in restaurants: 양이 많아요 ('the portions are generous') vs 그릇이 커요 ('the bowl is big') — both compliments, different claims.

Related split: 빠르다 (fast — speed) vs 이르다 (early — time position): 빠른 차 (a fast car), 이른 아침 (an early morning). And 길다 (long in length) vs 오래되다/오래 (long in time): 긴 머리 (long hair), 오래 기다렸어요 (waited a long time).

English adjectives sprawl across size/quantity/speed/time with one word each ('big', 'long'); Korean assigns each dimension its own adjective. When translating 'big/much/long', first ask 'which dimension?' — that question is the whole skill.
Give me a survival script for ordering food in a Korean restaurant, start to finish.

Enter and you will hear 어서 오세요 ('welcome'). Seat yourself or wait; to call staff, raise a hand and say 여기요! or 저기요! — both are normal; a bell on the table (벨) is even more normal.

Ordering: 이거 하나 주세요 ('one of this, please'), 김치찌개 두 개 주세요 ('two kimchi stews'), 덜 맵게 해 주세요 ('make it less spicy, please'), 안 맵게 해 주세요 for none at all. 계란 빼고 주세요 ('without egg, please') handles exclusions. 물 좀 주세요 ('water, please') — many places are self-service for water, watch for 물은 셀프예요 signs.

Mid-meal: 반찬 더 주세요 ('more side dishes, please' — banchan refills are free and expected), 공기밥 하나 더 주세요 ('one more bowl of rice').

Paying: 계산해 주세요 ('check, please'), 카드 돼요? ('do cards work?'), 따로 계산해 주세요 ('split the bill, please') or 같이 계산해 주세요. To-go: 포장해 주세요 ('please pack it to go').

Leave with 잘 먹었습니다 to the staff if someone treated you, or a simple 감사합니다. Notice the whole script runs on 주세요 — the polite request form does nearly all the work; vocabulary for dishes is the only variable.
Weather small talk — what do Koreans actually say, beyond 덥다 and 춥다?

Weather is Korea's default small talk, and the vocabulary is seasonal theater. Heat: 덥다 (hot), 후텁지근하다 (humid and muggy — the monsoon word), 푹푹 찐다 (steaming, said of July streets). Cold: 춥다, 쌀쌀하다 (chilly, crisp — early autumn praise), 매섭다 (biting, of wind). Rain: 비가 와요 (it's raining), 장마 (the summer monsoon season itself), 소나기 (a sudden shower), 부슬부슬 (drizzling texture word). Snow: 눈이 와요, 함박눈 (big fluffy flakes), 첫눈 (first snow — culturally loaded, romantic).

The verbs matter: rain and snow 'come' (오다), wind 'blows' (바람이 불어요), the sun 'is strong' (햇빛이 강해요), and weather ' 풀리다' means a cold snap relents: 날씨가 풀렸어요 ('the weather has softened').

Standard exchanges: 오늘 날씨 좋네요 ('nice weather today' — with that -네요 reaction ending), 요즘 왜 이렇게 더워요? ('why is it so hot these days?'), 감기 조심하세요 ('take care not to catch a cold' — the standard parting in cold snaps).

And the four-season pride is real: 한국은 사계절이 뚜렷해요 ('Korea has four distinct seasons') is a sentence you will hear as national small talk — agreeing warmly is the correct move.
'-거든요'는 어떤 상황에서 쓰나요? 드라마에서 정말 많이 들어요.

'-거든요'는 상대가 모르는 이유나 배경을 설명할 때 쓰는 표현이에요. 상대가 '왜?'라고 묻지 않아도, 먼저 이유를 꺼낼 때 자연스러워요. 예를 들어 약속을 거절할 때 '죄송해요. 제가 오늘 야근이 있거든요'라고 하면, 야근 때문에 안 된다는 배경을 부드럽게 설명하는 거예요.

새로운 정보를 소개할 때도 써요. '저 사실은 부산 출신이거든요'처럼 상대가 몰랐던 사실을 꺼내면서 대화를 시작할 수 있어요. 그래서 '-거든요'로 끝나는 문장은 보통 대화의 끝이 아니라, 다음 이야기를 여는 문장이에요. 상대의 반응이나 다음 질문을 기다리는 느낌이 있어요.

반대로 이미 아는 사실을 다시 말할 때는 '-잖아요'를 써요. '어제 말했잖아요'는 상대도 아는 사실을 상기시키는 표현이라, 가끔은 가벼운 핀잔처럼 들리기도 해요.

'-거든요'는 말하는 사람의 사정을 부드럽게 전하기 때문에, 거절이나 설명이 필요한 상황에서 아주 유용해요. 다만 글로 쓸 때는 거의 쓰지 않고, 말할 때 주로 쓰는 표현이에요.
Translating 'you' and 'please' into Korean keeps breaking my sentences. Are there really no equivalents?

Really — and your sentences are breaking at exactly the right places, because English builds politeness and address into words, while Korean builds them into grammar. 'You': Korean avoids pronouns for addressees — use the person's title (선생님, 사장님), name + 씨, a kinship term (언니, 아저씨), or nothing at all. 가세요? with no subject asks 'are you going?' perfectly. 당신 exists but is confrontational or spousal; 너 is intimate-downward only.

'Please': there is no freestanding 'please' word. Politeness rides on the request forms themselves: 주세요 (give me / do for me) is already polite — 물 주세요 is a complete, courteous 'water, please'. Add 좀 for softness: 물 좀 주세요 ('some water, please' — 좀 makes it smaller and gentler). Formal requests go up: 해 주시겠어요? ('would you do...?'), 부탁드립니다 ('I request your favor').

The mirror-image traps: 'thank you' before receiving (미리 감사합니다 is fine), and 'sorry' as attention-getter — use 실례합니다 or 저기요, not 미안합니다, to flag down a stranger.

Once you stop hunting for word-equivalents and start choosing relationship-settings, Korean politeness clicks: every ending is a dial, every omitted pronoun is information, and 'please' is something your verb does, not something your sentence carries.
Take this casual exchange and upgrade it twice — once to polite 해요체 and once to formal business Korean. A: 뭐 해? B: 밥 먹어. 같이 먹자. A: 좋아. 이따 전화해.

Here is the same exchange at three altitudes:

| Line | 반말 (friends) | 해요체 (polite) | 합쇼체 (formal) |
|---|---|---|---|
| What are you doing? | 뭐 해? | 뭐 해요? | 무엇을 하고 계세요? |
| I'm eating. | 밥 먹어. | 밥 먹어요. | 식사 중입니다. |
| Let's eat together. | 같이 먹자. | 같이 먹어요. | 함께 식사하시죠. |
| Sounds good. | 좋아. | 좋아요. | 좋습니다. |
| I'll call you later. | 이따 전화해. | 이따 전화할게요. | 나중에 전화드리겠습니다. |

Watch what changed besides endings. 'Eat' upgraded from 밥 먹다 to 식사하다 (the Sino-Korean formal word for dining) and then took the honorific -시- because the formal version honors the listener's action: 하고 계세요, 식사하시죠. The promise 'I'll call' climbed the humble ladder: 전화해 → 전화할게요 → 전화드리겠습니다, gaining 드리다 because the call benefits an elevated receiver.

Also note what did not change: no 'you' appears at any level, word order is identical, and the content is untouched. Register in Korean is a set of dials on the same machine — pronouns (absent throughout), noun choice (밥 → 식사), verb choice (먹다 → 드리다-forms), and endings. Turning all four dials together is what 'formal Korean' actually is.
